title: Writing Kernel with AI
text:
Welcome to Kernel Engineering
Accelerated computing and modern artificial intelligence rest on a single engineering discipline: extracting peak theoretical throughput from hardware.
Whether training frontier foundation models or serving millions of concurrent inference tokens, the software stack converges onto specialized computational kernels. Writing fast kernels is not a matter of guesswork or trial-and-error—it is an empirical science governed by the physics of computation: arithmetic intensity, memory bandwidth, latency hiding, and hardware execution hierarchies.

The Trajectory of This Book
This curriculum spans six rigorous parts designed to take you from first principles to the cutting edge:

Part I: Parallelism, from the CPU up: Understand how modern CPUs achieve massive throughput via SIMD vectorization and multi-threading before stepping into the GPU execution hierarchy: warps, streaming multiprocessors, memory coalescing, and the Roofline model.
Part II: The GEMM Worklog: Naive → cuBLAS: Master General Matrix Multiply (GEMM)—the operation that comprises over 90% of deep learning FLOPs. Step by step, elevate a naive kernel achieving 1.3% of GPU capacity to a hierarchical warp-tiled and Tensor Core (WMMA) implementation rivaling NVIDIA’s cuBLAS library.
Part III: Attention & Profiling: Diagnose hardware bottlenecks using NVIDIA Nsight Compute like a compiler engineer. Construct FlashAttention v1 from scratch, utilizing the online softmax algorithm to eliminate high-bandwidth memory bottlenecks.
Part IV: The Modern Frontier: Explore modern production kernels running on Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) architectures: FlashAttention-2/3/4, TMA asynchronous copy, WGMMA, Triton, CUTLASS, CuTe-DSL, PagedAttention, and NVFP4.
Part V: AI-Written Kernels: Analyze DeepSeek’s ultra-compact, high-performance kernels (FlashMLA and DeepGEMM). Step into the future of kernel development: using autonomous LLM agents (e.g., DeepMind AlphaEvolve, KernelBench) with profiler-in-the-loop guidance.
Part VI: Kernel Engineering Capstone Projects: Put your skills into practice with industry-grade capstone specifications developed with Crusoe, complete with verification harnesses, performance benchmarks, and demo-day technical presentations.

title: Parallelism on the CPU
text:
Parallelism on the CPU
Before programming thousands of lockstep cores on a GPU, we must build a mechanical understanding of how modern CPUs execute concurrent and parallel work. High-performance computing is fundamentally an exercise in orchestrating physical execution units while feeding them data fast enough to prevent pipeline stalls.
Modern CPUs extract performance across three distinct tiers of parallelism: 1. Instruction-Level Parallelism (ILP): Pipelining, superscalar dispatch, out-of-order execution, and branch prediction within a single core. 2. Data-Level Parallelism (SIMD): Single Instruction, Multiple Data execution where one machine instruction operates over a register packed with multiple independent values. 3. Thread-Level Parallelism (TLP): Multiple independent execution streams running concurrently across physical and logical processor cores.

title: Parallelism on the CPU
text:
1. Instruction-Level Parallelism (ILP) and Microarchitecture
A modern CPU core is not a simple sequential state machine. It is an asynchronous processing pipeline designed to retire multiple micro-operations (uops) per clock cycle.
       +--------------------------------------------------------+
       |                  Fetch & Branch Predict                |
       +---------------------------+----------------------------+
                                   |
       +---------------------------v----------------------------+
       |                  Decode & Macro-Op Fusion              |
       +---------------------------+----------------------------+
                                   |
       +---------------------------v----------------------------+
       |          Register Alias Table (RAT) & Rename           |
       +---------------------------+----------------------------+
                                   |
       +---------------------------v----------------------------+
       |            Reorder Buffer (ROB) & Reservation          |
       +-------+------------+------------+------------+---------+
               |            |            |            |
          +----v----+  +----v----+  +----v----+  +----v----+
          | ALU Port|  | ALU Port|  | SIMD/FMA|  |Load/Store|
          +---------+  +---------+  +---------+  +---------+

The Out-of-Order Engine

Instruction Fetch & Branch Prediction: The CPU fetches instructions ahead of the current program counter using branch target buffers (BTB) and direction predictors. When a branch is mispredicted, the entire speculative pipeline must be flushed, costing 15 to 20 cycles of wasted energy.
Decode and Micro-op Generation: Complex x86 instructions are broken down into simpler, RISC-like micro-operations (uops).
Register Renaming & Reservation Stations: To break false register dependencies (Write-After-Read and Write-After-Write hazards), the CPU maps architectural registers (e.g., rax, ymm0) to a much larger pool of physical registers.
Out-of-Order (OoO) Dispatch: Independent instructions whose operands are ready in the cache or register file execute out of program order across parallel execution ports.
In-Order Retirement: The Reorder Buffer (ROB) ensures that memory state updates and architectural register commits happen in strict program order, guaranteeing consistent exception semantics.

text:
3. Thread-Level Parallelism: Heavyweight vs Lightweight
To leverage multi-core CPUs, applications distribute work across threads. How threads are modeled dramatically impacts context switching overhead and memory footprint.
OS Heavyweight Threads:
  [Kernel Scheduler] ---> [Core 0: OS Thread (2-8 MB Stack)]  (Switch: ~1-3 us)
                     ---> [Core 1: OS Thread (2-8 MB Stack)]

Lightweight User-Space Green Threads / Fibers:
  [OS Thread / SM]    ---> [Fiber A (2 KB)] -> [Fiber B (2 KB)] -> [Fiber C (2 KB)]

The Cost of OS Threads
POSIX threads (pthread_create) or OpenMP workers (#pragma omp parallel for) allocate their own kernel task structure and a fixed memory stack (typically 2 MB to 8 MB). - When an OS thread context switches, the CPU must switch privilege rings into the kernel, save and restore architectural register state (including wide AVX-512 state), and suffer TLB and cache pollution. - Total latency: 1,000 to 3,000 CPU cycles (1–3 microseconds).


User-Space Concurrency (M:N Models)
Modern programming environments decouple logical concurrency from physical OS threads: - Go Goroutines: Allocate a dynamic 2 KB stack that grows on demand. The runtime multiplexes thousands of goroutines across a fixed thread pool (GOMAXPROCS), switching in user space within ~10 to 50 nanoseconds. - Java Virtual Threads (Project Loom): Suspendable continuation objects stored on the garbage-collected heap. - Rust Tokio: Futures compiled into zero-allocation state machines driven by a lock-free work-stealing executor.

title: Roofline Lab: Predict Then Measure
text:
Roofline Lab: Predict Then Measure
Every high-performance kernel is bounded by one of two physical constraints: 1. Compute Bound: The execution units (ALUs, FPUs, Tensor Cores) are saturated executing instructions; the memory interface has idle bandwidth. 2. Memory Bound: The execution units starve waiting for data to arrive from off-chip DRAM (HBM or GDDR); arithmetic throughput is a fraction of hardware peak.
Before writing a single line of CUDA, a kernel engineer must predict which regime the workload inhabits. Writing faster assembly or unrolling loops inside a memory-bound kernel achieves zero speedup. Conversely, optimizing memory tiling for a kernel already compute-bound yields diminishing returns.

title: Roofline Lab: Predict Then Measure
text:
1. The Roofline Model Formulation
The Roofline Model, formulated by Williams et al. (Berkeley), visualizes maximum achievable performance as a function of Operational Intensity (also called Arithmetic Intensity).

Definitions
\[\text{Operational Intensity } (I) = \frac{\text{Total Arithmetic Operations (FLOPs)}}{\text{Total Bytes Transferred from DRAM (Bytes)}}\]
\[\text{Attainable Performance } (P) = \min\left(\text{Peak Hardware Compute } (P_{\text{peak}}), \text{Peak Memory Bandwidth } (B) \times I\right)\]
Performance (TFLOP/s)
  ^
  |                           Peak Hardware Compute (P_peak)
  |                       +--------------------------------------- (Compute Bound)
  |                      /
  |                     /
  |                    /  Memory Bandwidth Slope
  |                   /   (P = Bandwidth * I)
  |                  /
  |                 /
  |                /      (Memory Bound)
  |               /
  +--------------+------------------------------------------------>
  0             I* (Ridge Point)         Operational Intensity (FLOPs/Byte)


The Ridge Point (\(I^*\))
The intersection between the memory bandwidth slope and the peak compute roof defines the Ridge Point (\(I^*\)):
\[I^* = \frac{P_{\text{peak}}}{B_{\text{peak}}}\]

If a workload’s intensity \(I < I^*\): The workload is strictly memory-bound. Maximum possible throughput is capped at \(B_{\text{peak}} \times I\). To go faster, you must reduce memory traffic (e.g. through kernel fusion or caching).
If a workload’s intensity \(I \ge I^*\): The workload is compute-bound. Maximum possible throughput is capped at \(P_{\text{peak}}\). To go faster, you must optimize instruction throughput, eliminate warp divergence, or switch to lower-precision numeric formats (e.g. FP16, BF16, FP8).

title: Roofline Lab: Predict Then Measure
text:
3. Dissecting Common Machine Learning Operations
Let us calculate the operational intensity for four fundamental deep learning operations executed on an NVIDIA A100 (SXM4: \(B = 2,039 \text{ GB/s}\), \(P_{\text{vector}} = 19.5 \text{ TFLOP/s}\)).

Case 1: Vector Addition (\(y = x + z\))
Given two vectors of length \(N = 10^7\) FP32 elements: - Operations: \(N\) additions = \(10^7\) FLOPs. - Memory Traffic: - Read \(x\): \(10^7 \times 4 \text{ B} = 40 \text{ MB}\). - Read \(z\): \(10^7 \times 4 \text{ B} = 40 \text{ MB}\). - Write \(y\): \(10^7 \times 4 \text{ B} = 40 \text{ MB}\). - Total Memory = \(120 \text{ MB} = 1.2 \times 10^8 \text{ Bytes}\). - Operational Intensity: \[I = \frac{10^7 \text{ FLOPs}}{1.2 \times 10^8 \text{ Bytes}} \approx 0.0833 \text{ FLOPs/Byte}\] - Analysis: \(I = 0.0833 \ll I^* = 9.6\). Strictly memory bound. - Maximum Theoretical Throughput: \[\text{Throughput} = 2,039 \text{ GB/s} \times 0.0833 \text{ FLOPs/Byte} \approx 169.8 \text{ GFLOP/s}\] The GPU achieves less than 0.9% of its FP32 compute capability. The ALU cores spend 99% of their time stalled waiting for memory controllers.


Case 2: LayerNorm / RMSNorm
RMSNorm computes: \(y_i = \frac{x_i}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2 + \epsilon}} \cdot \gamma_i\). For a hidden dimension \(d = 4096\): - Operations per token: - Square: \(d\) FLOPs. - Sum reduction: \(d - 1\) FLOPs. - Mean, add \(\epsilon\), reciprocal square root (rsqrt): \(\sim 4\) FLOPs. - Scale by \(\gamma\) and write: \(2d\) FLOPs. - Total \(\approx 4d \approx 16,384\) FLOPs. - Memory per token (unfused naive PyTorch): - Read input \(x\): \(d \times 4 \text{ B} = 16 \text{ KB}\). - Intermediates written and re-read from global memory: \(\sim 3 \times 16 \text{ KB} = 48 \text{ KB}\). - Write output \(y\): \(16 \text{ KB}\). - Total \(\sim 80 \text{ KB}\). - Operational Intensity: \[I = \frac{16,384 \text{ FLOPs}}{81,920 \text{ Bytes}} \approx 0.20 \text{ FLOPs/Byte}\] - Analysis: Completely memory bound. This is why fused normalization kernels (which keep intermediates in registers and shared memory) deliver massive 5x to 10x speedups.


Case 3: Dense Matrix Multiplication (GEMM)
Compute \(C = A \times B\) where \(A, B, C \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\), with \(M = K = N = 4096\): - Operations: \(2 \times M \times N \times K = 2 \times 4096^3 \approx 137.4 \times 10^9 \text{ FLOPs}\) (137.4 GFLOPs). - Minimum Algorithmic Memory (I/O): - Read \(A\): \(4096^2 \times 4 \text{ B} = 67.1 \text{ MB}\). - Read \(B\): \(4096^2 \times 4 \text{ B} = 67.1 \text{ MB}\). - Write \(C\): \(4096^2 \times 4 \text{ B} = 67.1 \text{ MB}\). - Total \(\approx 201.3 \text{ MB}\). - Operational Intensity (with perfect reuse): \[I_{\text{optimal}} = \frac{1.374 \times 10^{11} \text{ FLOPs}}{2.013 \times 10^8 \text{ Bytes}} \approx 682.6 \text{ FLOPs/Byte}\] - Analysis: \(I = 682.6 > I^* = 9.6\) (and even \(> I^*_{\text{Tensor}} = 153.0\)). Dense GEMM is thoroughly compute-bound when memory reuse is leveraged via shared memory tiling!

text:
4. The Multi-Tier Roofline (Hierarchy of Limits)
Modern GPUs have multiple memory tiers. A kernel that exhausts L2 cache bandwidth or shared memory bandwidth hits an intermediate roofline before reaching DRAM:
Throughput (TFLOP/s)
  ^
  |                                      Tensor Core Peak (989 TFLOP/s)
  |                       +--------------------------------------------
  |                      / (SM SRAM Bandwidth: ~19 TB/s)
  |                     /
  |                    /  (L2 Cache Bandwidth: ~5.2 TB/s)
  |                   /
  |                  /   (HBM3 DRAM Bandwidth: ~3.35 TB/s)
  |                 /
  +----------------+--------------------------------------------------->
  0                                        Operational Intensity (FLOPs/B)

HBM / DRAM Bandwidth: The slowest and largest layer. Optimization goal: load each byte from DRAM exactly once into on-chip memory.
L2 Cache Bandwidth: Over 2x to 3x faster than DRAM. Shared across all SMs.
Shared Memory / L1 SRAM Bandwidth: Over 5x to 8x faster than DRAM (~19 TB/s aggregate on H100). Serves warps inside a single SM.
Register File Bandwidth: Over 30 TB/s aggregate bandwidth. The only memory tier that can feed execution units at full single-cycle latency.

By comparing these two percentages, you instantly know whether to optimize memory access patterns or computational instructions.

title: The CUDA Programming Model & GPU Puzzles
text:
The CUDA Programming Model & GPU Puzzles
Modern GPUs execute programs using the SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) execution model. While SIMD on a CPU executes a single vector instruction over vector registers on a single core, SIMT executes hundreds of independent scalar threads grouped into lockstep units called warps.
Writing effective CUDA kernels requires understanding both the logical programming abstractions and how the hardware scheduler physically maps them onto silicon.

title: The CUDA Programming Model & GPU Puzzles
text:
1. The Logical vs Physical Hierarchy
CUDA defines a hierarchical programming model that scales seamlessly from a single-SM embedded chip (e.g. Jetson) to a massive data-center accelerator with 144 SMs (e.g. Hopper H100).
Logical Abstraction                     Physical Hardware
-------------------                     -----------------
Grid (Entire Kernel Launch)   ------>   GPU Device
  |
  +--> Thread Block (Cooperative) --->   Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)
         |
         +--> Warp (32 Threads)  ----->   Warp Scheduler & Execution Units
                |
                +--> Thread     ----->   CUDA Core / Register Slice

The Dimensions

Thread: The finest unit of execution. Each thread has its own program counter, private registers, and local memory stack.
Warp: A contiguous group of 32 threads. The warp is the fundamental unit of scheduling on the GPU. All 32 threads in a warp execute the same instruction simultaneously.
Thread Block (CTA - Cooperative Thread Array): A group of up to 1,024 threads. Threads within the same block reside on the same physical SM, share fast on-chip Shared Memory (SRAM), and can synchronize using barrier primitives (__syncthreads()).
Grid: The full set of thread blocks dispatched to execute a kernel. Thread blocks within a grid execute independently; there is no guaranteed execution order across blocks.

title: The CUDA Programming Model & GPU Puzzles
The CUDA Programming Model & GPU Puzzles
section: 3. Warp Divergence and the SIMT Execution Mask
text:
3. Warp Divergence and the SIMT Execution Mask
All 32 threads in a warp share a single instruction unit. If threads within a warp take different execution paths at a conditional branch (if / else), the hardware executes every branch path sequentially, disabling threads that are not on that path via a hardware execution mask.
Instruction Stream:
Thread 0-15:   Takes IF branch (condition is true)
Thread 16-31:  Takes ELSE branch (condition is false)

Execution Timeline:
Cycle 1-10:  [Thread 0-15 Active] [Thread 16-31 MASKED OFF] -> Executes IF body
Cycle 11-20: [Thread 0-15 MASKED OFF] [Thread 16-31 Active] -> Executes ELSE body
Reconverge:  [All Threads 0-31 Active]

The Cost of Divergence

When a warp diverges 2-ways, execution time roughly doubles.
When 32 threads take 32 distinct branch paths (e.g. switch(threadIdx.x % 32)), the warp serializes into 32 separate execution passes, dropping warp computational throughput to 3.1% of peak.



Best Practices to Eliminate Divergence

Align branches by warp boundary: Branches that depend strictly on blockIdx or threadIdx.x / 32 cause zero divergence because all 32 threads in the warp evaluate to the exact same condition.
Predicated Instructions: For tiny branches (1-2 instructions), the compiler automatically uses predicated instructions instead of jumping.
Use Intrinsic Math Primitives: Replace if (a < b) val = a; else val = b; with fminf(a, b), which compiles to a single non-branching instruction.

The Memory Hierarchy in Anger: Matrix Transpose
Writing fast GPU kernels is fundamentally about choreographing data movement through the memory hierarchy. While modern GPUs boast tens of teraflops of arithmetic power, every floating-point operation is useless if data cannot reach the functional units.
In this chapter, we dissect the GPU memory hierarchy, master global memory coalescing, resolve shared memory bank conflicts, and walk through the canonical optimization benchmark: Matrix Transpose.

title: The Memory Hierarchy in Anger: Matrix Transpose
text:
2. Global Memory Coalescing: The 10x Lever
When threads in a warp issue a read or write instruction to global memory, the memory controller does not process 32 separate individual 4-byte requests. Instead, it aggregates adjacent addresses into coalesced 32-byte or 128-byte memory transactions.

The Golden Rule of Coalescing

Consecutive threads in a warp (threadIdx.x from 0 to 31) must access consecutive memory addresses (address + 0, address + 4, …, address + 124).

Coalesced Access (Consecutive):
Threads:      T0   T1   T2   T3   ...  T31
               |    |    |    |         |
Memory Addr: 0x00 0x04 0x08 0x0C  ...  0x7C
Result: ONE single 128-byte transaction! (100% bus utilization)

Uncoalesced Strided Access (Column-wise):
Threads:      T0         T1         T2   ...  T31
               |          |          |         |
Memory Addr: 0x0000     0x1000     0x2000 ... 0x1F000 (Stride = N elements)
Result: 32 SEPARATE 32-byte transactions! (3.1% bus utilization!)
In the uncoalesced case, the GPU fetches \(32 \times 32 \text{ Bytes} = 1024 \text{ Bytes}\) over the physical memory bus to retrieve only \(32 \times 4 \text{ Bytes} = 128 \text{ Bytes}\) of useful data. 90% of your memory bandwidth is wasted.

title: The Memory Hierarchy in Anger: Matrix Transpose
text:
3. Shared Memory Bank Conflicts
Shared memory is organized into 32 independent memory banks, each with a word width of 4 bytes (32 bits).
Successive 32-bit words are assigned to successive banks in round-robin fashion: - bank_index = (byte_address / 4) % 32
Bank 0:  Word 0,  Word 32, Word 64 ...
Bank 1:  Word 1,  Word 33, Word 65 ...
...
Bank 31: Word 31, Word 63, Word 95 ...

The Conflict Condition

Conflict-Free: All 32 threads in a warp access different banks (or all threads broadcast-read the exact same word). The memory request completes in 1 cycle.
N-Way Bank Conflict: If \(N\) threads in a warp request different addresses that map to the same bank, the hardware must serialize the requests into \(N\) successive single-bank accesses. An 8-way conflict reduces shared memory throughput by \(8\times\).

title: GEMM Worklog I: Naive to Tiled
text:
GEMM Worklog I: Naive to Tiled
General Matrix Multiply (GEMM) is the computational engine of modern artificial intelligence. Fully connected layers, multi-head attention projections, convolutional layers (via im2col), and mixture-of-experts routers all compile down to GEMM:
\[C = \alpha (A \times B) + \beta C\]
where \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times K}\), \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times N}\), and \(C \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\).
In this worklog, we embark on the canonical kernel engineering journey: elevating a naive GEMM achieving less than 1.5% of GPU capacity to a shared-memory tiled kernel achieving over 36% of theoretical peak compute.

title: GEMM Worklog I: Naive to Tiled
section: 2. The Breakthrough: Shared Memory 2D Block Tiling
text:
2. The Breakthrough: Shared Memory 2D Block Tiling
To escape the memory bottleneck, we must reuse loaded data.
Notice: - All threads in the same row \(i\) need the exact same value \(A_{i,k}\). - All threads in the same column \(j\) need the exact same value \(B_{k,j}\).
Instead of streaming from global memory for every multiply-add, thread blocks load a 2D tile of \(A\) and a 2D tile of \(B\) into ultra-fast on-chip Shared Memory (SRAM), synchronize, and then perform multiple arithmetic operations from SRAM.
               Global Memory (Slow HBM)
                     |
           (Coalesced Block Load)
                     v
             Shared Memory Tile
         s_a [TILE x TILE]   s_b [TILE x TILE]
                     |
       (All threads reuse data TILE times!)
                     v
             Registers & ALUs

Tile Dimensions and Reuse Factor
With a tile size of \(\text{TILE} = 32\): - Each thread loads 1 element of \(A\) and 1 element of \(B\) into shared memory. - During the inner multiplication loop, each loaded element is read and reused by 32 separate threads! - Global memory traffic drops by a factor of \(32\times\). - Operational intensity jumps from \(0.25 \text{ FLOPs/Byte}\) to: \[I_{\text{tiled}} = 0.25 \times 32 = \mathbf{8.0 \text{ FLOPs/Byte}}\]
At \(8.0 \text{ FLOPs/Byte}\), we are right next to the hardware Ridge Point (\(I^* = 9.6\)).

title: GEMM Worklog II: Registers & Warp Tiling
text:
GEMM Worklog II: Registers & Warp Tiling
While shared memory tiling dramatically cuts DRAM traffic, shared memory bandwidth itself becomes the bottleneck at high utilization. Reaching near-cuBLAS performance requires register tiling and vectorized memory instructions.

Micro-Tiling in Registers
Registers provide ~20 TB/s aggregate bandwidth. Instead of each thread calculating a single output element \(C_{i,j}\), each thread computes a \(TM imes TN\) block of elements (e.g. \(8 imes 8 = 64\) values per thread).


Vectorized Memory Loads with float4
Global and shared memory loads should be widened using 128-bit vector loads (float4 / int4):
// Load 4 consecutive floats in a single 128-bit transaction
float4 a_val = *reinterpret_cast<const float4*>(&A[idx]);


The Warptiling Hierarchy
Modern production kernels decompose matrix multiply into four distinct structural layers: 1. Grid Tile: Handled by the entire GPU grid across all SMs. 2. Block Tile: Handled by a single thread block using shared memory. 3. Warp Tile: Handled by a 32-thread warp executing synchronized sub-tiles. 4. Thread Tile: Handled by individual thread registers.
By structuring the kernel into a \(128 imes 128\) block tile and \(64 imes 64\) warp tiles with double buffering, manual register allocation reaches 93.7% of cuBLAS speed on NVIDIA Ampere hardware.

Profiling & Debugging Like a Pro
text:
Profiling & Debugging Like a Pro
Optimization without profiling is speculation. Top kernel engineers diagnose bottlenecks systematically using the NVIDIA toolchain:

The Professional Diagnostic Stack

compute-sanitizer: Traps out-of-bounds memory accesses, misaligned memory addresses, uninitialized shared memory, and warp synchronization race conditions.
NVIDIA Nsight Systems (NSYS): Timeline visualization across CPU threads, CUDA streams, memory transfers, and kernel durations.
NVIDIA Nsight Compute (NCU): Deep architectural profiling inside individual kernels—analyzing warp stall reasons, SM issue pipe utilization, memory chart traffic, and register spills.



Debugging Sabotaged Kernels: 3 Classic Incident Scenarios

Incident 1: Silent Race Condition in Shared Memory: Threads write to s_data[threadIdx.x] and read from s_data[threadIdx.x + 1] without an intervening __syncthreads(). Detection: compute-sanitizer --tool racecheck ./my_kernel
Incident 2: Shared Memory Bank Conflicts: All 32 threads in a warp access different rows in the same shared memory bank simultaneously. Detection: NCU metric l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu_mem_shared.sum. Resolution: Stride padding (__shared__ float smem[32][33]).
Incident 3: Catastrophic Register Spilling: Kernel uses 80 registers per thread when the hardware limit per thread at target occupancy is 64. Excessive variables spill to local DRAM memory, increasing latency 100x. Detection: Compiler flag --ptxas-options=-v reporting spill stores / spill loads. Resolution: Kernel launch bound annotation __launch_bounds__(256, 2).

title: launch_bounds and Register Pressure: What the Compiler Picks When You Say Nothing
text:
launch_bounds and Register Pressure: What the Compiler Picks When You Say Nothing
The profiling chapter listed __launch_bounds__ as the fix for register spills. That is half the story, and the less useful half. Registers are the one resource the compiler allocates before it knows how you will launch the kernel. When you give ptxas no launch bounds, it does not know your block size. It optimises the kernel on its own terms, and it can produce a binary that cannot be launched at the block size you wanted, or that runs at 12% occupancy without anything telling you. __launch_bounds__(maxThreadsPerBlock, minBlocksPerSM) is a contract: it tells the register allocator how many threads must fit, and from that it derives a per-thread register cap.
This chapter compiles one register-hungry kernel five ways, reads the ptxas -v report for each, turns register counts into occupancy with a twenty-line calculator, and ends with the prompt pattern that keeps an AI assistant from “fixing” spills in the wrong direction.
Versions used: NVRTC 12.9 and ptxas 12.9.86 (nvidia-cuda-nvrtc-cu12, nvidia-cuda-nvcc-cu12 wheels), target sm_90 (H100), Python 3.13.5, Debian 13 x86-64. There is no GPU on the build machine: everything here is compile-time evidence, and outputs are pasted from the runs. Runtime speed is not measured, and Section 5 says what you must measure on hardware.

title: launch_bounds and Register Pressure: What the Compiler Picks When You Say Nothing
section: 1. Mental model: registers are divided, not shared
text:
1. Mental model: registers are divided, not shared
 one sm_90 SM: 65,536 32-bit registers, at most 64 resident warps (2,048 threads)

 regs/thread  →  regs/warp (×32, rounded up to 256)  →  warps that fit  →  occupancy
     32              1,024                               64                100 %
     64              2,048                               32                 50 %
    167              5,376                               12 → 8 (whole blocks of 8 warps)  12.5 %
    255              8,192                                8                 12.5 %

 __launch_bounds__(T, B)  ⇒  ptxas must fit B blocks of T threads on one SM
                          ⇒  cap ≈ 65,536 / (T·B), rounded down to the allocation unit
More registers per thread means fewer threads resident, which leaves less latency hiding. Fewer registers means spills to local memory (L1/L2-backed, so slow on a miss). The compiler balances these, but only against the constraint you give it.

launch_bounds and Register Pressure: What the Compiler Picks When You Say Nothing
section: 3. Compile five ways without a GPU
text:
3. Compile five ways without a GPU
NVRTC turns CUDA C++ into PTX in-process. ptxas -v then does register allocation for a real SM and reports the result. Neither step needs a device.
# build.py — CUDA C++ -> PTX with NVRTC (no GPU needed), then ptxas -v for register counts
import ctypes, subprocess, sys
NV = "/workspace/cudavenv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/nvidia"
nvrtc = ctypes.CDLL(f"{NV}/cuda_nvrtc/lib/libnvrtc.so.12")
def ptx(src, opts):
    prog = ctypes.c_void_p()
    assert nvrtc.nvrtcCreateProgram(ctypes.byref(prog), src.encode(), b"kernel.cu", 0, None, None) == 0
    arr = (ctypes.c_char_p * len(opts))(*[o.encode() for o in opts])
    rc = nvrtc.nvrtcCompileProgram(prog, len(opts), arr)
    size = ctypes.c_size_t(); nvrtc.nvrtcGetProgramLogSize(prog, ctypes.byref(size))
    log = ctypes.create_string_buffer(size.value); nvrtc.nvrtcGetProgramLog(prog, log)
    if rc: sys.exit(log.value.decode())
    nvrtc.nvrtcGetPTXSize(prog, ctypes.byref(size))
    out = ctypes.create_string_buffer(size.value); nvrtc.nvrtcGetPTX(prog, out)
    return out.value.decode()
src = open("kernel.cu").read()
variants = {
    "none":          [],
    "lb(256)":       ["-DBOUNDS=__launch_bounds__(256)"],
    "lb(1024)":      ["-DBOUNDS=__launch_bounds__(1024)"],
    "lb(256,4)":     ["-DBOUNDS=__launch_bounds__(256,4)"],
    "lb(1024,2)":    ["-DBOUNDS=__launch_bounds__(1024,2)"],
}
for name, extra in variants.items():
    p = ptx(src, ["--gpu-architecture=compute_90"] + extra)
    open(f"k_{name}.ptx", "w").write(p)
    r = subprocess.run([f"{NV}/cuda_nvcc/bin/ptxas", "-arch=sm_90", "-v", f"k_{name}.ptx", "-o", "/dev/null"],
                       capture_output=True, text=True)
    line = [l for l in r.stderr.splitlines() if "registers" in l or "spill" in l]
    print(f"{name:11s}", " | ".join(l.split("info    : ")[-1] for l in line))
    if name != "none":
        print(" "*11, [l.strip() for l in p.splitlines() if l.strip().startswith((".maxntid", ".minnctapersm", ".maxnreg"))])
$ python3 build.py
none            0 bytes stack frame, 0 bytes spill stores, 0 bytes spill loads | Used 167 registers, used 0 barriers
lb(256)         0 bytes stack frame, 0 bytes spill stores, 0 bytes spill loads | Used 200 registers, used 0 barriers
            ['.maxntid 256, 1, 1']
lb(1024)        1384 bytes stack frame, 3168 bytes spill stores, 3208 bytes spill loads | Used 64 registers, used 0 barriers, 1384 bytes cumulative stack size
            ['.maxntid 1024, 1, 1']
lb(256,4)       1384 bytes stack frame, 3168 bytes spill stores, 3208 bytes spill loads | Used 64 registers, used 0 barriers, 1384 bytes cumulative stack size
            ['.maxntid 256, 1, 1', '.minnctapersm 4']
lb(1024,2)      1912 bytes stack frame, 4452 bytes spill stores, 4628 bytes spill loads | Used 32 registers, used 0 barriers, 1912 bytes cumulative stack size
            ['.maxntid 1024, 1, 1', '.minnctapersm 2']
Read it row by row:

none: 167 registers, no spills. With no bounds, ptxas is free to use up to 255 registers per thread and picks what it thinks is fastest for one thread. Nothing in the binary records a block-size limit.
lb(256): 200 registers. Bounds can raise register use. 256 threads × 255 registers fits in 65,536, so the cap is loose, and ptxas spends more registers for its own scheduling heuristics. The exact choice is the compiler’s and can change between releases. .maxntid 256 is now in the PTX, and a launch with more than 256 threads is rejected.
lb(1024) and lb(256,4): 64 registers, 3.1 KB of spills per thread. Both ask for 1,024 resident threads per SM, so the cap is 65,536 / 1,024 = 64. The cost appears as spill stores/spill loads and a 1,384-byte stack frame.
lb(1024,2): 32 registers, 4.4 KB of spills. Two 1,024-thread blocks per SM means 2,048 threads, so the cap is 32.

-maxrregcount is the blunt, file-wide version of the same cap. It is passed to ptxas, and it overrides the per-kernel limit:
$ ptxas -arch=sm_90 -v -maxrregcount=64 k_none.ptx -o /dev/null
ptxas info    : Overriding maximum register limit 256 for 'poly_eval' with  64 of maxrregcount option
    1384 bytes stack frame, 3168 bytes spill stores, 3208 bytes spill loads
ptxas info    : Used 64 registers, used 0 barriers, 1384 bytes cumulative stack size
Prefer __launch_bounds__. It sets the cap per kernel, records it in the binary, and makes over-sized launches fail loudly.

title: launch_bounds and Register Pressure: What the Compiler Picks When You Say Nothing
text:
4. From register counts to occupancy
# occupancy.py — registers -> resident warps on one sm_90 SM (register limit only)
REGS_PER_SM, MAX_WARPS, MAX_BLOCKS, UNIT = 65536, 64, 32, 256    # H100 / sm_90 limits

def warps_resident(regs_per_thread, threads_per_block):
    per_warp = -(-regs_per_thread * 32 // UNIT) * UNIT            # round up to 256-reg units
    warps_per_block = -(-threads_per_block // 32)
    if per_warp * warps_per_block > REGS_PER_SM:
        return None                                               # launch fails: too many resources
    blocks = min(REGS_PER_SM // (per_warp * warps_per_block), MAX_BLOCKS,
                 MAX_WARPS // warps_per_block)
    return blocks * warps_per_block

rows = [("none", 167, 256), ("none", 167, 512), ("lb(256)", 200, 256),
        ("lb(256,4)", 64, 256), ("lb(1024)", 64, 1024), ("lb(1024,2)", 32, 1024)]
print(f"{'variant':11s} {'regs':>4s} {'block':>5s}  resident warps  occupancy")
for name, regs, block in rows:
    w = warps_resident(regs, block)
    print(f"{name:11s} {regs:4d} {block:5d}  " +
          ("launch FAILS (too many resources requested)" if w is None else f"{w:14d}  {w/MAX_WARPS:8.1%}"))
$ python3 occupancy.py
variant     regs block  resident warps  occupancy
none         167   256               8     12.5%
none         167   512  launch FAILS (too many resources requested)
lb(256)      200   256               8     12.5%
lb(256,4)     64   256              32     50.0%
lb(1024)      64  1024              32     50.0%
lb(1024,2)    32  1024              64    100.0%
The second row is the trap this chapter is named for. The unbounded build, launched with 512 threads per block, needs 16 warps × 5,376 registers = 86,016 registers in one block, and the SM has 65,536. The launch fails with cudaErrorLaunchOutOfResources (“too many resources requested for launch”). Code that worked at 256 threads breaks when someone tunes the block size, and nothing at compile time warned about it.
This calculator models the register limit only. Shared memory, the 32-blocks-per-SM limit and per-architecture allocation rules can bind first. On hardware, cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor and Nsight Compute’s Occupancy section are the authorities.

section: 5. Which build is fastest? Measure; don’t infer
text:
5. Which build is fastest? Measure; don’t infer
Occupancy is a means, not the goal. For this kernel the 167-register build has no spills and low occupancy. The 32-register build has full occupancy and more than 4 KB of local-memory traffic per thread. Which one wins depends on whether the kernel is latency-bound or bandwidth-bound and whether the spills stay in L1. On a GPU, run each variant at its own legal block size and compare with Nsight Compute (launch__registers_per_thread, sm__warps_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active, l1tex__t_bytes_pipe_lsu_mem_local_op_ld.sum, plus duration). The compile-time table tells you what you are trading. Only the profiler tells you what the trade is worth.

title: launch_bounds and Register Pressure: What the Compiler Picks When You Say Nothing
section: 6. The trap: “fixing” spills by removing the bounds
text:
6. The trap: “fixing” spills by removing the bounds
An assistant shown a ptxas log with spills will very often suggest deleting __launch_bounds__ or raising -maxrregcount. In this chapter’s terms that moves from the lb(1024) row to the none row. The spills disappear, and so does the guarantee that 1,024-thread blocks can launch. If the host code launches 1,024 threads, the “optimised” kernel now fails at runtime. Spills are a symptom. The bound encodes a launch decision that lives in host code the assistant may never have seen.

section: 7. Prompting an AI assistant for register work
text:
7. Prompting an AI assistant for register work
Give the model the constraint, the evidence, and a definition of done:
Kernel: poly_eval (attached). Target sm_90. Host launches 1024 threads/block; this is fixed.
Keep __launch_bounds__(1024). Current ptxas -v: 64 regs, 3168 B spill stores, 3208 B spill loads.
Goal: reduce spill bytes without changing the bound or the numerical result.
Allowed: restructure live ranges (fewer simultaneously live acc[] values), change unrolling.
Report: the ptxas -v line before and after, and a CPU reference check on 1e5 random inputs.
This rules out the bound-removal “fix”, forces an apples-to-apples ptxas comparison, and keeps correctness inside the definition of done.

Pitfalls

Reading Used N registers without the spill line on the same report.
Setting minBlocksPerSM from a wish rather than from what shared memory allows. If shared memory already limits you to 2 blocks, asking for 4 only adds spills.
Assuming register counts carry across architectures. Re-run ptxas -v for every -arch you ship.
Global -maxrregcount in a build file silently capping kernels that never needed it.

title: Attention: The Kernel That Ate the World & FlashAttention v1
text:
Attention: The Kernel That Ate the World & FlashAttention v1
Standard Transformer Attention computes:
\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{Softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V\]
For a sequence length \(N\) and head dimension \(d\) (\(N \gg d\)): - \(S = Q K^T\) generates an \(N \times N\) attention score matrix. - Traditional PyTorch implementations materialize \(S\) and \(P = \text{Softmax}(S)\) in global HBM memory (\(O(N^2)\) memory reads and writes). - For long contexts (\(N = 32k\) or \(128k\)), intermediate matrices consume gigabytes of memory and choke HBM bandwidth.

The Breakthrough: Online Softmax & Tiling
Tri Dao et al. introduced FlashAttention: compute the exact attention output without ever writing the \(N \times N\) intermediate attention matrix to global memory.
Traditional Attention (Memory-Bound):
  Q, K -> [Global HBM Write: S] -> [Global HBM Read: S] -> Softmax -> [Global HBM Write: P] -> [Global HBM Read: P] -> V -> Output
FlashAttention (Fused into SRAM):
  Load Blocks of Q, K, V into On-chip SRAM -> Compute Local Gemm -> Online Softmax Update -> Accumulate Output -> Single Global Write


The Online Softmax Formula
Traditional softmax requires two passes over the sequence: pass 1 to find the maximum \(m = \max(x_i)\), and pass 2 to compute \(\sum e^{x_i - m}\). Online softmax updates the running maximum \(m\) and normalization sum \(l\) incrementally as blocks stream through shared memory:
\[m_{\text{new}} = \max(m_{\text{prev}}, m_{\text{block}})\]
\[l_{\text{new}} = e^{m_{\text{prev}} - m_{\text{new}}} l_{\text{prev}} + e^{m_{\text{block}} - m_{\text{new}}} l_{\text{block}}\]
\[O_{\text{new}} = e^{m_{\text{prev}} - m_{\text{new}}} O_{\text{prev}} + P_{\text{block}} V_{\text{block}}\]

FlashAttention Evolution

FlashAttention-1 (2022): Proved that fusing attention and computing online softmax in SRAM yields 2-4x wall-clock speedups while cutting memory footprint from \(O(N^2)\) to \(O(N)\).
FlashAttention-2 (2023):

Swapped the outer and inner loops (looping over blocks of \(Q\) in the outer loop, streaming \(K, V\) in the inner loop).
Reduced non-matmul FLOPs by deferring output scaling until the very end.
Introduced sequence parallel work distribution across thread blocks.

FlashAttention-3 (2024):

Architected specifically for NVIDIA Hopper (H100) hardware.
Utilizes asynchronous Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) hardware pipelines.
Leverages Hopper WGMMA (Warp Group Matrix Multiply and Accumulate) instructions.
Implements FP8 mixed precision with low quantization error.

title: Beating cuBLAS on an H100
text:
Beating cuBLAS on an H100
NVIDIA’s Hopper H100 microarchitecture introduced two revolutionary hardware subsystems:

1. Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA)
In pre-Hopper architectures, threads in a warp explicitly load data from global memory into registers, then write from registers into shared memory. TMA executes multidimensional tensor transfers (e.g. 2D/3D tiles) directly between global HBM and shared memory asynchronously in hardware, completely bypassing the register file and consuming zero SM ALU cycles.


2. Warp Specialization
Instead of every thread in a block performing both memory loading and arithmetic: - Producer Warps (1-2 warps): Issue asynchronous TMA copy instructions to fetch upcoming tiles into double-buffered shared memory. - Consumer Warps (Warp Groups): Execute continuous WGMMA matrix multiply instructions without ever pausing for memory latency. - Hardware barrier arrive/wait primitives (cuda::barrier) synchronize producers and consumers with cycle-level precision.

title: Triton → CUTLASS → CuTe-DSL
text:
Triton → CUTLASS → CuTe-DSL
Kernel engineering in 2025-2026 has transitioned from hand-written CUDA C++ toward declarative and high-level DSL frameworks.

OpenAI Triton
Triton allows writing high-performance GPU kernels in idiomatic Python. The programmer writes code at the granularity of block tiles rather than individual threads. The Triton compiler handles intra-block scheduling, memory coalescing, and shared memory allocation automatically.
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, output_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE
    offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    tl.store(output_ptr + offsets, x + y, mask=mask)


CUTLASS & CuTe
NVIDIA CUTLASS 3.x is structured around CuTe: a C++ template library that unifies data layouts, coordinates, and hierarchical tensor tiling through mathematical layout algebra: \[  ext{Layout} = ( ext{Shape},     ext{Stride})\]

title: Inference-Serving Kernels
text:
Inference-Serving Kernels
LLM inference splits into two distinct execution regimes with radically different performance characteristics: 1. Prefill Phase: The prompt is processed in parallel. High operational intensity, strictly compute-bound. 2. Decode Phase: Tokens are generated autoregressively one by one. The model loads billions of weights to compute a single new vector. Strictly memory-bound!

PagedAttention (vLLM)
In standard inference, KV caches must be allocated as contiguous memory buffers. This leads to 60-80% memory waste due to internal and external memory fragmentation. PagedAttention treats KV cache memory like virtual memory pages in an operating system: - KV vectors are stored in non-contiguous 16-token page blocks. - A page table maps logical token positions to physical GPU memory addresses. - Result: Memory waste drops to near 0%, enabling 2-4x higher serving concurrency on the same hardware.

title: Blackwell & NVFP4
text:
Blackwell & NVFP4
NVIDIA’s Blackwell (B200 / GB200) microarchitecture represents the state of the art in frontier hardware (2025-2026).

Blackwell Architectural Highlights

tcgen05 Tensor Cores: 5th generation Tensor Cores delivering 4x higher FP4 training and inference density compared to Hopper FP8.
Tensor Memory (TMEM): A dedicated ultra-fast on-chip memory structure decoupled from shared memory, specifically optimized for multi-tensor staging and GEMM accumulation.
NVFP4 Microscopic Scaling: 4-bit floating point format with micro-block scaling factors that preserves accuracy across large foundation models while doubling token throughput.

title: A Blackwell GEMM by Hand in CuTe DSL: TMA, mbarriers, TMEM, and tcgen05
text:
A Blackwell GEMM by Hand in CuTe DSL: TMA, mbarriers, TMEM, and tcgen05
On Blackwell (B200, GB200, sm_100a) the tensor core no longer accumulates into registers. A single thread issues tcgen05.mma, which reads both operands from shared memory and accumulates into Tensor Memory (TMEM), a 256 KB per-SM scratchpad owned by the tensor core. Operands arrive by TMA, an asynchronous copy engine driven by one thread and a descriptor. Everything is coordinated by mbarriers whose phase bits you track by hand. To write a fast GEMM, you have to keep this asynchronous machinery fed.
This chapter builds that GEMM from the raw primitives in NVIDIA’s CuTe DSL (the Python front end to CUTLASS’s CuTe), without the pipeline helper classes, so that every barrier and phase flip is visible. It uses a public step-by-step optimization ladder on a B200, from 164 to about 1400 TFLOP/s on a 4096³ FP16 problem (97% of cuBLAS), as a map. The ladder shows which steps mattered and why three of them did nothing.
What was and was not run. No Blackwell GPU was available for this chapter. Everything that can run without one did run: the kernel below is cross-compiled for sm_100a on a CPU-only machine, and the generated PTX, SASS and register counts are inspected. Shared-memory bank behavior is modeled in Python, and the roofline and budget arithmetic is computed. The kernel has not been executed, and every timing in this chapter is a measurement reported by the write-up’s author, labeled as such. Treat the kernel as a compile-verified teaching listing and check it against a GPU before relying on it. NVIDIA’s tutorial fp16_gemm_0.py is the tested reference with the same structure.
Toolchain used: Debian 13.7, Python 3.13.5, nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0, and the ptxas/nvdisasm shipped with Triton 3.8.0 (CUDA 13.3 tools).

title: A Blackwell GEMM by Hand in CuTe DSL: TMA, mbarriers, TMEM, and tcgen05
text:
1. Two regimes: prefill and decode
A GEMM \(C_{M\times N} = A_{M\times K} B_{N\times K}^\top\) does \(2MNK\) FLOPs and moves at least \(2(MK + NK + MN)\) bytes in FP16. When \(N\) and \(K\) are large the ratio is about \(M\) FLOP per byte. In LLM inference, \(M\) is the number of tokens in the batch: thousands in prefill, tens to hundreds in decode. That single number decides the bottleneck.
# file: gemm_math.py
# Back-of-envelope numbers for an FP16 GEMM on a B200-class GPU: roofline per shape,
# shared-memory stage budget, pipeline depth from latency, and wave counts.
# Kernel/cuBLAS times are the ones REPORTED in the write-up that inspired this chapter
# (B200, fp16, CUDA events); they were not measured here.
PEAK_TFLOPS = 1500        # cuBLAS-achievable fp16 dense, as reported; not the datasheet peak
HBM_TBS = 7.7             # achievable HBM bandwidth, as reported
SMS = 148
SMEM_MAX = 227 * 1024     # max dynamic shared memory per block on sm_100 (CuTe DSL capacity map)

shapes = {  # name: (M, N, K, reported_us_kernel, reported_us_cublas)
    "square 4096^3":         (4096, 4096, 4096, 98.0, 94.9),
    "prefill attn-out":      (8192, 8192, 8192, 816, 741),
    "prefill MLP up":        (8192, 28672, 8192, 2934, 2407),
    "decode MLP up":         (256, 28672, 8192, 113, 111),
    "decode MLP down":       (256, 8192, 28672, 138, 112),
    "decode fused QKV":      (256, 10240, 8192, 52, 38),
    "decode attn-out":       (256, 8192, 8192, 48, 32),
}
print("1) roofline (bytes = A + B + C once, fp16)")
print(f"{'shape':18} {'FLOP/B':>7} {'bound':>7} {'floor us':>8} {'kernel us':>9} {'TFLOP/s':>7} "
      f"{'TB/s':>5} {'cuBLAS us':>9} {'ratio':>5} {'CTAs':>5} {'waves':>5}")
for name, (M, N, K, t, tc) in shapes.items():
    flop, byt = 2 * M * N * K, 2 * (M * K + N * K + M * N)
    t_c, t_m = flop / PEAK_TFLOPS / 1e6, byt / HBM_TBS / 1e6       # microseconds
    ctas = (M // 128) * (N // 256)                                  # 128x256 tile per CTA
    print(f"{name:18} {flop / byt:7.0f} {'compute' if t_c > t_m else 'memory':>7} {max(t_c, t_m):8.1f} "
          f"{t:9.1f} {flop / t / 1e6:7.0f} {byt / t / 1e6:5.2f} {tc:9.1f} {tc / t:5.2f} "
          f"{ctas:5d} {ctas / SMS:5.2f}")
print(f"ridge point: {PEAK_TFLOPS / HBM_TBS:.0f} FLOP/B")

print("\n2) shared memory per pipeline stage (tile_k = 64, fp16)")
for label, a_rows, b_rows in (("1-CTA 128x256", 128, 256), ("2-CTA 256x256, per CTA", 128, 128)):
    stage = (a_rows + b_rows) * 64 * 2
    flop = 2 * 128 * 256 * 64                  # each CTA still accumulates 128x256 per k-step
    print(f"{label:24} {stage // 1024:3d} KiB/stage  {flop / stage:5.1f} FLOP per SMEM byte  "
          f"max stages in 227 KiB: {SMEM_MAX // stage}")

print("\n3) stages needed to cover load latency (Little's law), 1-CTA 128x256x64 k-step")
t_step = 2 * 128 * 256 * 64 / (PEAK_TFLOPS * 1e12 / SMS) * 1e6     # us per k-step at peak
for lat in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0):
    print(f"  latency {lat:3.1f} us: k-step {t_step:.2f} us -> need >= {1 + lat / t_step:4.1f} stages")

print("\n4) the reported ladder at 4096^3 (cuBLAS 94.9 us)")
ladder = [("1 K-loop, 1 stage, tile_k 16", 840), ("2 4-stage ring", 448),
          ("3 warp specialization", 449), ("4 tile_k 64 + 128B swizzle", 110),
          ("5 pipelined epilogue", 110), ("6 TMA multicast 2x2", 109.4),
          ("7 2-CTA MMA (256-row)", 107.3), ("8 persistent + 2 TMEM slots", 98.0)]
prev = None
for name, us in ladder:
    tf = 2 * 4096**3 / us / 1e6
    step = "" if prev is None else f"{prev / us:5.2f}x"
    print(f"  {name:30} {us:6.1f} us {tf:6.0f} TFLOP/s {94.9 / us:5.2f} of cuBLAS {step}")
    prev = us

Prefill is deep in compute-bound territory (1300–3600 FLOP/B against a ridge near 195). The game is keeping the tensor pipe busy.
Decode at M=256 sits right at the ridge (about 245 FLOP/B), so both bandwidth and compute matter. The decisive column is waves. Decode attention-output launches 64 CTAs on 148 SMs, 0.43 waves, so more than half the machine idles no matter how good the inner loop is. The reported 2.97 TB/s against roughly 4.4 TB/s for cuBLAS is what that looks like.
Decode batches below 256 are worse still for this kernel: its 2-CTA tile is 256 rows tall, so M must be padded to 256.

title: A Blackwell GEMM by Hand in CuTe DSL: TMA, mbarriers, TMEM, and tcgen05
section: 2. The data path and the four primitives
text:
2. The data path and the four primitives
          TMA (1 thread, async)          tcgen05.mma (1 thread, async)        tcgen05.ld (4 warps)
 GMEM ──────────────────────────► SMEM ring ────────────────────────► TMEM ─────────────────────► RF ──► GMEM
 A[M,K], B[N,K]            stage 0 │ stage 1 │ … │ stage S-1          128 lanes × 512 cols      fp32 → fp16
                            ▲ full[s] (tx bytes)   empty[s] ▲           (accumulator)
                            └──── producer warp ◄──────────┘ MMA warp ── commit ──► acc_full ──► epilogue
TMA. One thread passes a descriptor (built on the host from the tensor’s shape, strides and the SMEM layout) and tile coordinates. The hardware copies the tile and decrements a byte count on an attached mbarrier as data lands. Address arithmetic, bounds and swizzling live in the descriptor, not in registers.
mbarrier. A 64-bit SMEM object holding an expected arrival count, a pending count, a transaction (byte) count and a phase bit. When arrivals and bytes both reach zero the phase flips and waiters are released. A wait names the phase it is waiting to see complete. A barrier reused once per lap around an \(S\)-stage ring therefore alternates phase 0, 1, 0, 1 by lap, and the code must track that parity. A wrong parity hangs the kernel on the second lap, or worse, passes early and reads stale data.
TMEM. 128 lanes × 512 columns of 32-bit cells per SM. A 128×256 FP32 accumulator uses 256 columns, so two fit. One warp allocates with tcgen05.alloc, which takes a power of two of at least 32 columns and writes the TMEM address to SMEM, and the same warp frees it at the end. The epilogue reads TMEM with tcgen05.ld, and each warp can reach only its own 32-lane quarter.
tcgen05.mma (UMMA). One thread issues an MMA of up to 128×256×16 (FP16) for one CTA, or 256×256×16 for a CTA pair. It reads SMEM through matrix descriptors and accumulates in TMEM. It is asynchronous. tcgen05.commit makes an mbarrier arrive when all previously issued MMAs have completed, which is how the MMA warp tells the producer “this stage is free” and the epilogue “the accumulator is final”.

title: A Blackwell GEMM by Hand in CuTe DSL: TMA, mbarriers, TMEM, and tcgen05
text:
3. The kernel
The listing below is a complete warp-specialized GEMM: a 128×256 output tile per CTA, a ring of STAGES shared-memory stages each TILE_K deep, warp 0 as the TMA producer, warp 1 as the MMA issuer, and all four warps in the epilogue. The three knobs are environment variables so that one file can be compiled in several configurations. The structure follows NVIDIA’s CuTe DSL Blackwell tutorial; the pipeline is written out with raw mbarrier calls.
# file: bw_gemm.py
# A warp-specialized Blackwell (sm_100a) FP16 GEMM in CuTe DSL, written against
# the raw primitives: TMA loads, mbarriers with explicit phases, tcgen05 MMA into
# Tensor Memory, and a TMEM -> register -> global epilogue.
#
#   C[M, N] = A[M, K] @ B[N, K]^T     (A and B both K-major, FP16 in, FP32 accumulate)
#
# Knobs (module-level, read by the host function at trace time):
#   STAGES    shared-memory ring depth for A/B tiles
#   TILE_K    K depth of one stage (16 = one MMA instruction, 64 = four)
#   ATOM      "sw128" (128-byte XOR swizzle) or "inter" (no swizzle)
import os

import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute
import cutlass.utils as utils
from cutlass.cute.nvgpu import cpasync, tcgen05

STAGES = int(os.environ.get("STAGES", 4))
TILE_K = int(os.environ.get("TILE_K", 64))
ATOM = os.environ.get("ATOM", "sw128")

io_dtype, acc_dtype = cutlass.Float16, cutlass.Float32
MMA_INST = (128, 256, 16)          # one tcgen05.mma.cta_group::1 kind::f16 instruction
TILER = (128, 256, TILE_K)         # one CTA's output tile and the K depth of a stage
THREADS = 128                      # 4 warps: 0 = TMA producer, 1 = MMA issuer, all = epilogue
TMEM_COLS = 256                    # FP32 128x256 accumulator = 256 TMEM columns


@cute.struct
class Barriers:
    full: cute.struct.MemRange[cutlass.Int64, STAGES]   # stage s holds fresh A/B bytes
    empty: cute.struct.MemRange[cutlass.Int64, STAGES]  # MMAs reading stage s have retired
    acc_full: cutlass.Int64                             # accumulator complete in TMEM
    tmem_slot: cutlass.Int32                            # tcgen05.alloc writes the TMEM address here


@cute.kernel
def gemm_kernel(tiled_mma: cute.TiledMma,
                tma_a: cute.CopyAtom, mA: cute.Tensor,
                tma_b: cute.CopyAtom, mB: cute.Tensor,
                mC: cute.Tensor,
                sA_layout: cute.ComposedLayout, sB_layout: cute.ComposedLayout,
                tx_bytes: cutlass.Constexpr):
    tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
    warp = cute.arch.make_warp_uniform(cute.arch.warp_idx())
    bm, bn, _ = cute.arch.block_idx()

    # ---- shared memory: barriers, then the swizzled A/B ring (1024 B aligned for SW128)
    smem = utils.SmemAllocator()
    bars = smem.allocate(Barriers)
    sA = smem.allocate_tensor(io_dtype, sA_layout.outer, byte_alignment=1024, swizzle=sA_layout.inner)
    sB = smem.allocate_tensor(io_dtype, sB_layout.outer, byte_alignment=1024, swizzle=sB_layout.inner)
    full, empty = bars.full.data_ptr(), bars.empty.data_ptr()
    acc_full = bars.acc_full.ptr

    if warp == 0:
        with cute.arch.elect_one():
            for s in cutlass.range_constexpr(STAGES):
                cute.arch.mbarrier_init(full + s, 1)    # one arrive (the producer) + tx bytes
                cute.arch.mbarrier_init(empty + s, 1)   # one arrive (tcgen05.commit)
                cute.arch.mbarrier_arrive(empty + s)    # pre-arm: every slot starts empty
            cute.arch.mbarrier_init(acc_full, 1)
        cpasync.prefetch_descriptor(tma_a)
        cpasync.prefetch_descriptor(tma_b)
        cute.arch.alloc_tmem(TMEM_COLS, bars.tmem_slot.ptr)   # warp-wide; result lands in SMEM
    cute.arch.mbarrier_init_fence()
    cute.arch.sync_threads()
    tmem_ptr = cute.arch.retrieve_tmem_ptr(acc_dtype, alignment=16,
                                           ptr_to_buffer_holding_addr=bars.tmem_slot.ptr)

    # ---- partition global tiles for this CTA and build MMA fragments over SMEM / TMEM
    coord = (bm, bn, None)
    gA = cute.local_tile(mA, TILER, coord, proj=(1, None, 1))     # (128, TILE_K, k_tiles)
    gB = cute.local_tile(mB, TILER, coord, proj=(None, 1, 1))     # (256, TILE_K, k_tiles)
    gC = cute.local_tile(mC, TILER, coord, proj=(1, 1, None))     # (128, 256)
    thr = tiled_mma.get_slice(0)
    tCgA, tCgB, tCgC = thr.partition_A(gA), thr.partition_B(gB), thr.partition_C(gC)
    tCrA, tCrB = tiled_mma.make_fragment_A(sA), tiled_mma.make_fragment_B(sB)
    acc = tiled_mma.make_fragment_C(tiled_mma.partition_shape_C(TILER[:2]))
    acc = cute.make_tensor(tmem_ptr, acc.layout)                  # the accumulator lives in TMEM

    tAsA, tAgA = cpasync.tma_partition(tma_a, 0, cute.make_layout(1),
                                       cute.group_modes(sA, 0, 3), cute.group_modes(tCgA, 0, 3))
    tBsB, tBgB = cpasync.tma_partition(tma_b, 0, cute.make_layout(1),
                                       cute.group_modes(sB, 0, 3), cute.group_modes(tCgB, 0, 3))
    k_tiles = cute.size(gA, mode=[2])

    if warp == 0:
        # ---- producer: wait for an empty slot, arm its full barrier with the byte count, issue TMA
        stage, phase = cutlass.Int32(0), cutlass.Int32(0)
        for k in cutlass.range(k_tiles, unroll=1):
            cute.arch.mbarrier_wait(empty + stage, phase)
            with cute.arch.elect_one():
                cute.arch.mbarrier_arrive_and_expect_tx(full + stage, tx_bytes)
            cute.copy(tma_a, tAgA[(None, k)], tAsA[(None, stage)], tma_bar_ptr=full + stage)
            cute.copy(tma_b, tBgB[(None, k)], tBsB[(None, stage)], tma_bar_ptr=full + stage)
            stage += 1
            if stage == STAGES:                  # wrapped the ring: the next wait is one phase later
                stage = cutlass.Int32(0)
                phase ^= 1
    elif warp == 1:
        # ---- MMA issuer: wait for a full slot, run TILE_K/16 MMAs, commit the slot back as empty
        stage, phase = cutlass.Int32(0), cutlass.Int32(0)
        tiled_mma.set(tcgen05.Field.ACCUMULATE, False)            # first MMA overwrites TMEM
        for k in cutlass.range(k_tiles, unroll=1):
            cute.arch.mbarrier_wait(full + stage, phase)
            for kb in cutlass.range_constexpr(cute.size(tCrA, mode=[2])):
                cute.gemm(tiled_mma, acc, tCrA[(None, None, kb, stage)],
                          tCrB[(None, None, kb, stage)], acc)
                tiled_mma.set(tcgen05.Field.ACCUMULATE, True)     # every later MMA adds
            with cute.arch.elect_one():
                tcgen05.commit(empty + stage)    # arrives when these MMAs have read the slot
            stage += 1
            if stage == STAGES:
                stage = cutlass.Int32(0)
                phase ^= 1
        with cute.arch.elect_one():
            tcgen05.commit(acc_full)             # arrives when every MMA has finished

    # ---- epilogue (all 128 threads): TMEM -> registers (32 lanes per warp) -> FP16 -> global
    cute.arch.mbarrier_wait(acc_full, 0)
    epi = ((cute.size(acc, mode=[0, 0]), cute.size(acc, mode=[0, 1]) // 4),)
    acc_epi, gC_epi = cute.zipped_divide(acc, epi), cute.zipped_divide(tCgC, epi)
    t2r = tcgen05.make_tmem_copy(cute.make_copy_atom(tcgen05.Ld32x32bOp(tcgen05.Repetition.x64),
                                                     acc_dtype), acc_epi[None, 0])
    t2r_thr = t2r.get_slice(tidx)
    src, dst = t2r_thr.partition_S(acc_epi), t2r_thr.partition_D(gC_epi)
    r_acc = cute.make_rmem_tensor(dst[None, None, 0].shape, acc_dtype)
    r_out = cute.make_rmem_tensor(dst[None, None, 0].shape, io_dtype)
    for i in cutlass.range_constexpr(cute.size(src, mode=[2])):
        cute.copy(t2r, src[None, None, i], r_acc)
        r_out.store(r_acc.load().to(io_dtype))
        cute.autovec_copy(r_out, dst[None, None, i])

    cute.arch.sync_threads()
    if warp == 0:
        cute.arch.relinquish_tmem_alloc_permit()
        cute.arch.dealloc_tmem(tmem_ptr, TMEM_COLS)


def smem_atom():
    kind = {"sw128": tcgen05.SmemLayoutAtomKind.K_SW128,
            "inter": tcgen05.SmemLayoutAtomKind.K_INTER}[ATOM]
    return tcgen05.make_smem_layout_atom(kind, io_dtype)


@cute.jit
def gemm(a: cute.Tensor, b: cute.Tensor, c: cute.Tensor):
    op = tcgen05.MmaF16BF16Op(io_dtype, acc_dtype, MMA_INST, tcgen05.CtaGroup.ONE,
                              tcgen05.OperandSource.SMEM,
                              tcgen05.OperandMajorMode.K, tcgen05.OperandMajorMode.K)
    tiled_mma = cute.make_tiled_mma(op)
    a_shape = cute.append(tiled_mma.partition_shape_A(cute.dice(TILER, (1, None, 1))), STAGES)
    b_shape = cute.append(tiled_mma.partition_shape_B(cute.dice(TILER, (None, 1, 1))), STAGES)
    sA_layout = tcgen05.tile_to_mma_shape(smem_atom(), a_shape, order=(1, 2, 3))
    sB_layout = tcgen05.tile_to_mma_shape(smem_atom(), b_shape, order=(1, 2, 3))
    one_a, one_b = cute.select(sA_layout, mode=[0, 1, 2]), cute.select(sB_layout, mode=[0, 1, 2])
    tma_op = cpasync.CopyBulkTensorTileG2SOp(tcgen05.CtaGroup.ONE)
    tma_a, tA = cute.nvgpu.make_tiled_tma_atom_A(tma_op, a, one_a, TILER, tiled_mma)
    tma_b, tB = cute.nvgpu.make_tiled_tma_atom_B(tma_op, b, one_b, TILER, tiled_mma)
    tx_bytes = cute.size_in_bytes(io_dtype, one_a) + cute.size_in_bytes(io_dtype, one_b)
    gemm_kernel(tiled_mma, tma_a, tA, tma_b, tB, c, sA_layout, sB_layout, tx_bytes).launch(
        grid=cute.ceil_div((*c.layout.shape, 1), TILER[:2]), block=(THREADS, 1, 1))
The parts worth slowing down for:

Pre-armed empty barriers. Each empty[s] is initialized with count 1 and immediately arrived on once, which completes its phase 0. On the first lap the producer waits for phase 0 and passes straight through, so no separate prologue loop is needed. On lap 2 it waits for phase 1, which completes only when tcgen05.commit(empty + s) fires after the MMAs that read stage s.
arrive_and_expect_tx before the copies. The producer arrives on full[s] and announces tx_bytes (A tile + B tile) in one call. The two TMA copies then count those bytes down. The consumer’s wait on full[s] cannot succeed until both the arrival and every byte have landed. If the byte count is wrong in either direction, the kernel hangs or races.
Phase flips on wrap, not per iteration. stage and phase advance together, and phase ^= 1 happens only when the ring wraps. Producer and consumer keep identical counters, which is what makes the protocol easy to reason about.
ACCUMULATE off for the first MMA only. TMEM is not zeroed. The first cute.gemm must overwrite and every later one must add, and the DSL does not toggle this for you.
The epilogue waits on one barrier. acc_full completes once, at phase 0, after the final commit. All 128 threads then pull 32 lanes per warp out of TMEM in four 64-column chunks, convert to FP16 and store. A production kernel stages through SMEM and uses a TMA store. This one stays short.
The swizzle rides on the pointer. allocate_tensor(..., swizzle=layout.inner) attaches the XOR function to the SMEM pointer and keeps the affine part (with the stage mode) as the layout, and the base is 1024-byte aligned. Passing a composed layout where the MMA fragment builder expects an affine one is rejected.

section: 4. Compile for sm_100a without a GPU
text:
4. Compile for sm_100a without a GPU
CuTe DSL can JIT-compile against fake tensors (shape, dtype, alignment, no memory) for a named architecture and dump the PTX and cubin. That catches a large class of errors (layout mismatches, illegal swizzle/tile combinations, type errors) and lets you read what the kernel will do.
# file: compile_check.py
# Cross-compile bw_gemm.py for sm_100a on a machine with no GPU and report what the
# compiler produced. Run once per configuration (the knobs are environment variables).
import os
import pathlib
import re
import sys

import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute
from cutlass.cute.runtime import make_fake_compact_tensor

import bw_gemm as g

M = N = K = 4096
out = pathlib.Path("build") / f"s{g.STAGES}_k{g.TILE_K}_{g.ATOM}"
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
fake = lambda r, c: make_fake_compact_tensor(cutlass.Float16, (r, c), stride_order=(1, 0),
                                             assumed_align=32)
try:
    cute.compile(g.gemm, fake(M, K), fake(N, K), fake(M, N),
                 options=f"--gpu-arch sm_100a --keep-ptx --keep-cubin --dump-dir {out}")
except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - report the compiler's verdict, whatever it is
    lines = [l.strip() for l in str(e).splitlines() if "error" in l] or [str(e).strip()]
    print(f"STAGES={g.STAGES} TILE_K={g.TILE_K:<2} ATOM={g.ATOM:<5}  REJECTED:\n    {lines[0][:150]}")
    sys.exit(0)

ptx = next(out.glob("*.ptx")).read_text()
count = lambda pat: len(re.findall(pat, ptx))
stage_bytes = (128 + 256) * g.TILE_K * 2
print(f"STAGES={g.STAGES} TILE_K={g.TILE_K:<2} ATOM={g.ATOM:<5}  ok  "
      f"smem/stage={stage_bytes // 1024} KiB ring={g.STAGES * stage_bytes // 1024} KiB  "
      f"tcgen05.mma={count(r'tcgen05\.mma')} tma.load={count(r'cp\.async\.bulk\.tensor')} "
      f"try_wait={count(r'mbarrier\.try_wait')} tcgen05.ld={count(r'tcgen05\.ld')}")

What the compiler is telling you:

The 128-byte swizzle cannot be used with a 16-deep tile. The SW128 atom is 8 rows × 64 FP16 (128 bytes) in K. A 16-deep stage cannot hold one, and layout algebra rejects the combination while building the TMA atom. This matches the write-up’s account that the swizzle “needs tile_k >= 64” and that tile_k 64 alone changed nothing. Each half of the winning change looks useless when tested alone.
Without swizzling, TMA moves 16-byte-wide boxes. The non-swizzled (“interleaved”) canonical layout is built from 8-row × 16-byte core matrices, so each operand’s 64-deep slice becomes eight narrow TMA boxes: 16 cp.async.bulk.tensor per stage against 2 with SW128.
MMA count per stage = TILE_K / 16: 1 at depth 16, 4 at depth 64. That is the work available to overlap each wait.
Six 48 KiB stages compile fine and cannot launch. 288 KiB exceeds the 227 KiB per-block limit on sm_100. Dynamic shared memory is sized at launch, so nothing at compile time objects. CuTe DSL inserts a launch-time check that prints an error, and the driver refuses the launch.

Then look at register use and the SASS:

B=build/s4_k64_sw128
$NV/ptxas-blackwell -arch=sm_100a -v $B/*.ptx -o /tmp/k.cubin 2>&1 | grep -E "registers|spill"
$NV/nvdisasm -c $B/*.cubin \
  | grep -oE '\b(UTCHMMA|UTMALDG|UTCBAR|LDTM\.x64|SYNCS\.[A-Z]+(\.[A-Z0-9]+)*)' | sort | uniq -c

      6 SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64.TRYWAIT

78 registers and no spills, because the accumulator is not in registers. The four UTCHMMA are the four tcgen05.mma per stage, UTMALDG are the two TMA loads, UTCBAR are the two commits (stage-empty and accumulator-full), LDTM.x64 are the four TMEM reads, and the SYNCS.* family is mbarrier init, arrive and try-wait. SASS opcode names are not documented by NVIDIA. This mapping is inferred by matching counts against the PTX.

Three things generalize beyond this kernel:

One change did most of the work, and it was a data-layout change. No amount of pipelining or specialization helps if the load path is serialized.
The nulls were predictable from the profile. At step 3, L1/TEX was at 98% and specialization does not reduce L1/TEX traffic. At step 6 the kernel was compute-bound, so cutting L2 reads could not help. Before each step, ask which counter the change will move and whether that counter is the binding one.
“L1TEX scoreboard” stalls in these kernels are mostly mbarrier waits. mbarrier.try_wait polls an SMEM word through the L1TEX pipe. In a healthy warp-specialized kernel every role waits for the role before it, so this stall grows as the kernel gets faster. Watch tensor-pipe utilization instead.

title: A Blackwell GEMM by Hand in CuTe DSL: TMA, mbarriers, TMEM, and tcgen05
text:
6. The swizzle
Shared memory has 32 banks of 4 bytes, so a 128-byte row covers each bank exactly once. If a tile’s row pitch is 128 bytes, the same column of every row falls in the same banks. A 128B swizzle (Swizzle<3,4,3> on byte addresses) XORs the 16-byte chunk index (address bits 4–6) with the row index mod 8 (bits 7–9). Rows keep their bytes, but chunks are permuted within each row so that a column hits eight different bank groups.
# file: swizzle_model.py
# Shared memory: 32 banks x 4 bytes. A 16-byte access covers 4 consecutive banks, so
# 8 such accesses can be served together if they hit 8 different 4-bank groups.
# Count how many serialized passes ("wavefronts") 8 rows x 16 bytes at the same logical
# column need, for plain and 128B-swizzled layouts, at two row pitches.
def sw128(addr):
    """CuTe Swizzle<3,4,3> on byte addresses: XOR bits [7,10) (row mod 8) into bits [4,7)
    (16-byte chunk within a 128-byte row)."""
    return addr ^ (((addr >> 7) & 0b111) << 4)


def passes(addrs):
    words_per_bank = {}
    for a in addrs:
        for w in range(4):                       # a 16-byte chunk = 4 consecutive 4-byte words
            word = a // 4 + w
            words_per_bank.setdefault(word % 32, set()).add(word)
    return max(len(s) for s in words_per_bank.values())


print(f"{'tile_k (fp16)':>13} {'row pitch':>9} {'layout':>8}  passes for 8 rows x 16 B, per column chunk")
for tile_k in (16, 64):
    pitch = tile_k * 2
    for name, f in (("plain", lambda a: a), ("sw128", sw128)):
        if name == "sw128" and pitch < 128:
            print(f"{tile_k:13d} {pitch:7d} B {name:>8}  n/a: needs 128-byte rows (tile_k >= 64)")
            continue
        per_col = [passes([f(r * pitch + c * 16) for r in range(8)]) for c in range(pitch // 16)]
        print(f"{tile_k:13d} {pitch:7d} B {name:>8}  {per_col}")

print("\nsw128 permutation of the eight 16-byte chunks, rows 0..7:")
for r in range(8):
    print(f"  row {r}: " + " ".join(str((sw128(r * 128 + c * 16) - r * 128) // 16) for c in range(8)))

With 128-byte rows and no swizzle, reading or writing one 16-byte column across 8 rows takes 8 serialized passes. With SW128 it takes 1. The write-up isolated the load path (no MMA) and reported 3.85 TB/s unswizzled against 18.5 TB/s swizzled, a 4.8x difference on TMA writes into SMEM. The exact access pattern TMA uses internally is not documented, so treat the model as the reason the canonical layouts exist, not a prediction of the exact ratio. Section 4 adds a second effect: the non-swizzled canonical layout forces TMA into eight 16-byte-wide boxes per operand per stage, many small requests where one large one would do. Both effects point the same way.
Rules that fall out of this: the K-major SW128 atom needs tile_k * sizeof(T) to be a multiple of 128 bytes (64 FP16 or BF16, 128 FP8). The SMEM base must be 1024-byte aligned (8 rows × 128 B, one full swizzle period). The TMA descriptor and the UMMA descriptor must agree on the swizzle mode. CuTe derives both from the same layout, which is the main reason to let it.

title: A Blackwell GEMM by Hand in CuTe DSL: TMA, mbarriers, TMEM, and tcgen05
section: 7. Stages: the budget and the regime
text:
7. Stages: the budget and the regime
Part 2 of gemm_math.py gives the hard limit. A 1-CTA 128×256×64 stage is 48 KiB, so at most 4 stages fit in 227 KiB. A 2-CTA tile halves each CTA’s B operand to 32 KiB, so up to 7 fit. NVIDIA’s tutorial fp16_gemm_1.py makes the same calculation in its docstring. Part 3 is Little’s law. At peak, one 64-deep k-step takes about 0.41 µs per SM, so the ring must hold \(1 + \text{latency}/0.41\,\mu s\) stages to hide load latency. That is 3–6 stages for 1–2 µs of loaded-system latency.
The write-up’s stage sweeps show why this has to be re-measured. At step 3 (16-deep stages), 4, 8 and 12 stages were flat (451.7, 454.6, 454.1 µs reported), because the kernel was not latency-bound. On the step-7 kernel (32 KiB stages) the same sweep went from 166.9 µs at 2 stages to a best of 105.9 µs at 5, and the shipped value of 6 was within noise. A sweep result holds only for the bottleneck that was active when you ran it.

text:
8. Two CTAs, then persistence
The last two rungs are where hand-written kernels usually stop matching the tutorials, and where the official examples are the best reference. Cross-compiling NVIDIA’s tutorial ladder shows the features appearing:
# file: official_check.py
# Cross-compile NVIDIA's CuTe DSL tutorial GEMMs (CUTLASS examples, BSD-3) for sm_100a
# and count the instructions that mark each feature: 1-CTA vs 2-CTA MMA, multicast TMA,
# cluster barriers, and TMA stores.

        "TMA multicast": r"cp\.async\.bulk\.tensor[^;]*multicast", "cluster barrier": r"barrier\.cluster",
        "tcgen05.alloc": r"tcgen05\.alloc", "TMA store": r"cp\.async\.bulk\.tensor\.\dd\.global\.shared"}

                 options=f"--gpu-arch sm_100a --keep-ptx --dump-dir {out}")

python official_check.py cutlass/examples/python/CuTeDSL/cute/blackwell/tutorial/tutorial_gemm \
    fp16_gemm_0 fp16_gemm_1 fp16_gemm_2 fp16_gemm_3
Output (CUTLASS at commit 0b55a2f):
tutorial     mma cta_group::1 mma cta_group::2    TMA multicast  cluster barrier    tcgen05.alloc        TMA store
fp16_gemm_0                 8                0                0                0                1                0
fp16_gemm_1                 0                8               14                4                1                0
fp16_gemm_2                 0                8                8                4                1                1
fp16_gemm_3                 0                8                8                6                1                1

2-CTA MMA (fp16_gemm_1). tcgen05.mma.cta_group::2 replaces cta_group::1. A cluster of two CTAs on neighboring SMs issues one 256-row MMA; each CTA supplies half of A, half of B and holds half the accumulator. Cluster barriers appear because the pair has to agree that both are initialized. The pair is not symmetric: the leader CTA alone waits on the full barrier, issues the MMA and commits, and tcgen05.commit signals only the CTAs named in its multicast mask. The write-up’s hang at this step came from a commit that never reached the follower’s empty barrier. It completed at K=192, where no stage is recycled, and hung at K=1024. Shrinking K until the hang disappears is a fast way to tell “stage reuse is broken” apart from “something else is broken”.
Warp specialization + TMA store (fp16_gemm_2). Same MMA, epilogue through SMEM and a TMA store.
Persistent (fp16_gemm_3). Launch one CTA (pair) per SM and loop over tiles with a tile scheduler. On its own that only removes launch and tail overhead. The real gain comes from two TMEM accumulator slots, 2 × 256 = all 512 columns. The MMA warp fills slot i % 2 while the epilogue drains the other, with an acc_full[s]/acc_empty[s] barrier pair per slot mirroring the A/B ring. The epilogue should release acc_empty[s] as soon as its tcgen05.lds complete, before converting and storing, so that the MMA warp gets the slot back early. Limits: N ≤ 256 per slot, the overlap only helps if the epilogue is shorter than the mainloop, and the first mainloop and last epilogue are never hidden.

The later tutorials add dynamic cluster-launch-control scheduling (fp16_gemm_3_1), preferred clusters (_4), TMA prefetch (_5) and programmatic dependent launch (_6). The write-up’s reported threadblock-swizzle experiment (grouping 8 tile rows so neighboring CTAs share B tiles in L2) reached parity with cuBLAS on a 4096×4096×16384 problem and did nothing at 4096³, where 512 CTAs is too few waves for ordering to matter.

section: 9. Why decode loses, and what to do about it
text:
9. Why decode loses, and what to do about it
The final reported comparison (part 1 of gemm_math.py) is 0.97x of cuBLAS on the square problem, 0.82–0.91x on prefill, and 0.67–0.98x on decode. The decode pattern follows the waves column:

MLP up (224 CTAs, 1.5 waves): 0.98x. Enough tiles to fill the machine. The kernel reads 478 MB from HBM, about the size of the 470 MB weight, so each weight is read once, at about 61% of peak DRAM bandwidth (reported).
Attention output and MLP down (64 CTAs, 0.43 waves): 0.67x and 0.81x. Fewer tiles than SMs. Persistence cannot help with less than one tile per CTA: the reported attention-output time was 47 µs before and after step 8.

The standard fixes:








Fix
What it does
Cost




Smaller N tiles (128 or 64)
More CTAs: 128 for N=8192 with 128-wide tiles
Lower arithmetic intensity per CTA; still ≥ ridge at M=256


Split-K
Each CTA reduces a K slice; a second pass or atomics combine
Extra FP32 partial traffic; nondeterminism with atomics


Stream-K
Persistent CTAs take equal shares of the total MAC-loop iterations, crossing tile boundaries
Fix-up logic for partial tiles; best general answer for odd shapes


1-CTA MMA for small M
Avoid padding M up to 256
Gives up the 2-CTA weight-tile sharing



cuBLAS picks among these per shape with heuristics. A hand-written kernel that only has one tiling will lose somewhere, which is why production libraries ship families of kernels and why the shape list should come from your model, not from the square.

section: 10. Driving an AI assistant through a ladder like this
text:
10. Driving an AI assistant through a ladder like this
The source write-up’s experiments were run by an AI coding agent under the author’s direction. That works well when the human enforces the method:

One change per step, timed on fixed shapes, with a correctness check in every run. The write-up’s threadblock-swizzle sweep produced a fake 1.13x speedup at swizzle_m=32, and its maximum error was 772: CTAs had walked off the end of M and skipped work. Any speedup without a passing comparison against torch.matmul is a bug report.
Size the prize before optimizing a stage. “The epilogue is at most 13 µs of 109” would have cancelled step 5 in advance. Ask the assistant to time each stage in isolation first: MMA-only (no loads), loads-only, epilogue-only. The write-up’s MMA-only ablation ran at 96.4 µs (cuBLAS speed) while loads-only took 417 µs, and that pair of numbers identified the bottleneck.
Make the assistant name the counter its change should move, and reject changes aimed at a counter that is not saturated.
Re-sweep knobs when the bottleneck moves. Stage count, tile shape and cluster shape all interact with it.
Have it compile for the target first. The cross-compile in Section 4 costs seconds and catches illegal layouts, shared-memory overflows and register spills before you pay for GPU time.

A prompt skeleton that encodes this:
You are optimizing a CuTe DSL GEMM for sm_100a. Current kernel: <file>. Shapes: <list>.
Rules: change ONE thing per step. Before editing, state which Nsight Compute metric you
expect to move and why it is the binding constraint now. After editing: cross-compile,
report registers/spills and SMEM bytes, then run the correctness check against torch
(state the max abs error and the tolerance; the reference write-up saw 0 for K<=8192 and 0.5 at K=28672) and time 50 iterations with CUDA events.
Report "no change" for differences under 2%. Never report a speedup without the error.
