11. Verification and benchmark plan

On a CPU (done here)

Cross-compile every configuration you intend to run. Reject anything over 227 KiB of SMEM, and check ptxas -v for spills.
Count PTX/SASS instructions per stage (MMAs, TMA loads, commits) against what the design says.



On a Blackwell GPU (not done here)

Correctness: random FP16 inputs, compare against torch.matmul with FP32 accumulation, for K ∈ {64, 192, 1024, 8192}. K=192 never recycles a 4-stage ring; K=1024 does, so it exposes phase bugs. Also test M and N not divisible by the tile and expect either a clean rejection or correct predication.
Timing: CUDA events around 20–50 iterations after warm-up, with torch.matmul on the same tensors in the same process. The write-up measured about 1.7 µs run-to-run spread, so treat differences under 2% as noise.
Profiling: Nsight Compute sm__pipe_tensor_op_* utilization, L1/TEX and DRAM throughput, waves per SM, and the stall breakdown. On cloud containers that cannot lock clocks, use --clock-control none and compare percentages across kernel versions, not absolutes.

title: A Blackwell GEMM by Hand in CuTe DSL: TMA, mbarriers, TMEM, and tcgen05
text:
Summary
A Blackwell GEMM is a small asynchronous system. TMA moves tiles into a shared-memory ring, mbarriers with explicit phases hand stages between a producer warp and a single-thread MMA issuer, tcgen05.mma accumulates in TMEM, and the epilogue drains TMEM through registers. The kernel in this chapter writes all of that out in CuTe DSL and is verified by cross-compiling for sm_100a. Its PTX and SASS contain exactly the MMAs, TMA loads, commits and TMEM loads the design calls for, with no spills. The ladder’s lessons are about method more than primitives. One layout change (tile_k 64 with a 128-byte swizzle) delivered a 4x gain, three plausible optimizations were null because they targeted counters that were not binding, and the final 2-CTA and persistent double-buffered steps closed the gap to cuBLAS on large shapes. Decode shapes are decided by waves, not by the inner loop, and need split-K, stream-K or smaller tiles. Compile for the target first, check correctness in every timing run, and re-measure whenever the bottleneck moves.

text:

title: Flash Attention 4
text:
Flash Attention 4

The 2026 Frontier: Breaking the 1 PFLOPS Single-GPU Barrier
On Blackwell hardware, Tensor Core matrix multiply units run so extraordinarily fast that the normalization step in Softmax—historically a minor fraction of runtime—becomes the dominant bottleneck.
FlashAttention-4 introduces Adaptive Softmax: - Dynamically checks divergence between running block maximums and candidate maximums. - Skips full re-normalization when numerical differences fall below precision thresholds. - Overlaps Softmax correction entirely behind asynchronous WGMMA execution pipelines. - Written using modern Python CuTe-DSL, FA4 is the first kernel to achieve over 1 PFLOPS of sustained attention compute on a single processor.

title: Jagged Flash Attention on Blackwell with TLX
text:
Jagged Flash Attention on Blackwell with TLX
Meta’s ads models (GEM, Kunlun) run attention over jagged user sequences: lengths that differ by orders of magnitude inside one batch. Padding them to a common L_max can waste half the FLOPs. The training stack instead packs tokens contiguously and stores an offsets tensor that marks each sequence’s boundaries. Jagged Flash Attention (JFA) is FlashAttention applied directly to that packed layout—never materializing padded tokens.
On Blackwell (B200), hitting peak throughput has meant hand-written CuTe-DSL or CUDA. In October 2026 the PyTorch/Meta team showed that TLX (Triton Low-level Extensions) closes much of that gap for JFA: about 3.2K lines of Triton-level code (roughly 3× less than FA4’s ~10K-line CuTe-DSL kernels), ~13% faster than FA4 (May 2026) on the forward jagged shapes that matter for ads, and ~50% faster on the backward—while staying readable enough for modeling engineers to fork into MXFP8 and block-sparse variants.
This chapter builds the mental model and the host-side pieces you can verify without a GPU: packing waste, a CPU online-softmax JFA that matches padded attention, zigzag tile balancing for skewed KV lengths, and the broadcast-Q backward bottleneck. TLX primitives (warp specialization, explicit SMEM/TMEM, CLC) are explained from the primary posts; we do not invent B200 timings. Versions: Python 3.13.5, PyTorch 2.14.1, Triton 3.8.0, ptxas from CUDA 12.9 wheels. No GPU on this box—TRITON_INTERPRET=1 for tiny kernels; JFA reference is pure PyTorch CPU.

title: Jagged Flash Attention on Blackwell with TLX
section: 2. Packing waste and a CPU JFA reference
text:
2. Packing waste and a CPU JFA reference
Save as jagged_attn_ref.py. It packs variable-length sequences, runs a blockwise online-softmax FlashAttention on the packed tensors, and checks against naïve padded attention.
# jagged_attn_ref.py — jagged (packed) FlashAttention reference on CPU
import math
import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)


def pack_sequences(seqs):
    offsets = [0]
    parts = []
    for s in seqs:
        parts.append(s)
        offsets.append(offsets[-1] + s.shape[0])
    return torch.cat(parts, dim=0), torch.tensor(offsets, dtype=torch.int32)


def attention_padded(q, k, v, lengths, causal=False):
    B, Lmax, D = q.shape
    scale = 1.0 / math.sqrt(D)
    out = torch.zeros_like(q)
    for b in range(B):
        L = lengths[b]
        qb, kb, vb = q[b, :L], k[b, :L], v[b, :L]
        scores = (qb @ kb.T) * scale
        if causal:
            mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(L, L, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1)
            scores = scores.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
        out[b, :L] = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1) @ vb
    return out


def jagged_flash_attention(q_pack, k_pack, v_pack, offsets, causal=False):
    """Online-softmax FlashAttention on packed sequences (single head)."""
    D = q_pack.shape[1]
    scale = 1.0 / math.sqrt(D)
    out = torch.empty_like(q_pack)
    B = offsets.numel() - 1
    BLOCK = 16
    for b in range(B):
        s, e = int(offsets[b]), int(offsets[b + 1])
        L = e - s
        for i0 in range(0, L, BLOCK):
            i1 = min(i0 + BLOCK, L)
            qi = q_pack[s + i0 : s + i1]
            bq = i1 - i0
            m_i = torch.full((bq,), float("-inf"))
            l_i = torch.zeros(bq)
            acc = torch.zeros(bq, D)
            for j0 in range(0, L, BLOCK):
                j1 = min(j0 + BLOCK, L)
                kj = k_pack[s + j0 : s + j1]
                vj = v_pack[s + j0 : s + j1]
                S = (qi @ kj.T) * scale
                if causal:
                    q_idx = torch.arange(i0, i1)[:, None]
                    k_idx = torch.arange(j0, j1)[None, :]
                    S = S.masked_fill(k_idx > q_idx, float("-inf"))
                m_ij = S.max(dim=-1).values
                m_new = torch.maximum(m_i, m_ij)
                alpha = torch.exp(m_i - m_new)
                P = torch.exp(S - m_new[:, None])
                l_new = alpha * l_i + P.sum(dim=-1)
                acc = acc * alpha[:, None] + P @ vj
                m_i, l_i = m_new, l_new
            out[s + i0 : s + i1] = acc / l_i[:, None]
    return out


def demo():
    D = 32
    lengths = [7, 3, 19, 5, 11]
    B, Lmax = len(lengths), max(lengths)
    seqs_q, seqs_k, seqs_v = [], [], []
    q_pad = torch.zeros(B, Lmax, D)
    k_pad = torch.zeros(B, Lmax, D)
    v_pad = torch.zeros(B, Lmax, D)
    for b, L in enumerate(lengths):
        q, k, v = torch.randn(L, D), torch.randn(L, D), torch.randn(L, D)
        seqs_q.append(q); seqs_k.append(k); seqs_v.append(v)
        q_pad[b, :L] = q; k_pad[b, :L] = k; v_pad[b, :L] = v
    q_pack, off = pack_sequences(seqs_q)
    k_pack, _ = pack_sequences(seqs_k)
    v_pack, _ = pack_sequences(seqs_v)

    print("lengths:", lengths)
    print("packed tokens:", int(off[-1]), "vs padded:", B * Lmax,
          f"(padding waste {(1 - off[-1].item() / (B * Lmax)) * 100:.1f}%)")

    for causal in (False, True):
        ref = attention_padded(q_pad, k_pad, v_pad, lengths, causal=causal)
        jag = jagged_flash_attention(q_pack, k_pack, v_pack, off, causal=causal)
        jag_pad = torch.zeros_like(q_pad)
        for b in range(B):
            s, e = int(off[b]), int(off[b + 1])
            jag_pad[b, : e - s] = jag[s:e]
        err = (ref - jag_pad).abs().max().item()
        print(f"causal={causal}: max|padded - jagged_flash| = {err:.3e}")

    # broadcast-Q sketch (dense Q vs each sequence's K/V)
    Lq, scale = 4, 1.0 / math.sqrt(D)
    q_dense = torch.randn(Lq, D)
    outs = []
    for b in range(B):
        s, e = int(off[b]), int(off[b + 1])
        scores = (q_dense @ k_pack[s:e].T) * scale
        outs.append(torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1) @ v_pack[s:e])
    stacked = torch.stack(outs, dim=0)
    print("broadcast-Q: Q", tuple(q_dense.shape),
          "per-seq outs", tuple(stacked.shape),
          "batch-mean", tuple(stacked.mean(0).shape))
    print("broadcast-Q note: backward dQ reduce-adds across the batch "
          "(contended epilogue in the TLX JFA post).")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo()

causal=True: max|padded - jagged_flash| = 4.768e-07

Fifty percent padding waste on a mild length mix is exactly why GEM packs. Equivalence at 1e-7 says the online-softmax recurrence is doing the same math as materializing \(P=\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top)\); the GPU kernel’s job is to keep tensor cores fed while doing it.

section: 3. Why plain Triton stalls on Blackwell
text:
3. Why plain Triton stalls on Blackwell
Attention reaches peak only when global loads, softmax, and matmuls overlap. A mature compiler-scheduled Triton JFA is algorithmically correct but leaves on-chip movement and warp roles to the compiler: one homogeneous warp group does loads, softmax, and MMAs, so tensor cores stall whenever that group is not issuing an MMA. Blackwell adds TMEM, async TMA, tcgen05 MMA, and Cluster Launch Control (CLC). Plain Triton does not expose them as first-class controls.
TLX adds explicit, hardware-aware primitives on top of Triton’s tile model: SMEM/TMEM allocation, async_task warp specialization, barriers, async TMA/MMA, and CLC. Meta’s structural rewrite splits a CTA into role-specialized tasks (TMA loads, tensor-core matmuls, softmax/correction, epilogue store, plus a dedicated dQ-reduction warp in backward), triple-buffers K/V, aliases TMEM buffers with non-overlapping lifetimes, and runs persistent CTAs (one per SM looping over tiles). That structure is what makes the §2.2 optimizations cheap to prototype in Python-level code instead of CuTe-DSL.

title: Jagged Flash Attention on Blackwell with TLX
section: 4. Host-side load balancing for jagged tiles
text:
4. Host-side load balancing for jagged tiles
Jagged lengths create SM imbalance: a few long sequences keep some SMs busy long after short ones finish. For the forward (outer loop over dense Q tiles, inner over jagged KV), tile cost ≈ KV length. Meta’s host heuristic: sort tiles by KV workload descending, then hand them to SMs in a zigzag (boustrophedon) pattern—even passes left-to-right, odd passes right-to-left. They report ~20% forward recovery from this alone.
# jagged_balance.py — zigzag vs round-robin tile assignment (host-side, no GPU)
import numpy as np


def zigzag_assign(workloads, n_sms):
    order = list(np.argsort(-np.asarray(workloads)))
    loads = np.zeros(n_sms, dtype=np.int64)
    assign = np.empty(len(workloads), dtype=np.int32)
    left_to_right, pos = True, 0
    while pos < len(order):
        indices = range(n_sms) if left_to_right else range(n_sms - 1, -1, -1)
        for sm in indices:
            if pos >= len(order):
                break
            t = order[pos]
            assign[t] = sm
            loads[sm] += workloads[t]
            pos += 1
        left_to_right = not left_to_right
    return assign, loads


def round_robin(workloads, n_sms):
    loads = np.zeros(n_sms, dtype=np.int64)
    assign = np.empty(len(workloads), dtype=np.int32)
    for t, w in enumerate(workloads):
        assign[t] = t % n_sms
        loads[t % n_sms] += w
    return assign, loads


rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n_tiles, n_sms = 48, 8
work = rng.integers(32, 512, size=n_tiles).astype(np.int64)
work[0], work[1], work[2] = 480, 450, 40
print("KV tile workloads: min", work.min(), "median", int(np.median(work)),
      "max", work.max(), f" max/median={work.max()/np.median(work):.1f}x")
_, loads_rr = round_robin(work, n_sms)
_, loads_zz = zigzag_assign(work, n_sms)


def stats(name, loads):
    print(f"{name:12s}  per-SM={loads.tolist()}")
    print(f"{'':12s}  max={loads.max()} mean={loads.mean():.1f}  "
          f"imbalance={loads.max()/loads.mean():.3f}  range={loads.max()-loads.min()}")


stats("round-robin", loads_rr)
stats("zigzag", loads_zz)
print("forward: zigzag by KV workload; backward: round-robin + CLC for residual skew.")
$ python jagged_balance.py
KV tile workloads: min 40 median 242 max 502  max/median=2.1x

              max=1937 mean=1569.5  imbalance=1.234  range=850

              max=1604 mean=1569.5  imbalance=1.022  range=59

Imbalance \(1.23\to 1.02\) is the whole point of the host sort. CLC then covers residual runtime variance: a persistent CTA steals the next tile index on demand when it finishes early. TLX exposes this as clc_create_context / clc_producer / clc_consumer (see the CLC+TLX post). Software balancing still matters on a CLC kernel because CLC cannot see empty padded tiles—host-side valid-tile precompute prunes those first.
The backward uses a different static policy: dK/dV tiles against shared dense Q are roughly equal cost, so round-robin with block-innermost ordering (L2 reuse) plus padding to cluster size for the 2-CTA path.

text:
Pitfalls

Padding as the default. If your batcher always pads to L_max, no attention kernel can recover the wasted FLOPs. Fix the layout first.
Testing only dense equal-length shapes. FA4 can win on long dense sequences; JFA’s wins are on jagged broadcast-Q. Benchmark the distribution you serve.
CLC without pruning empty tiles. Dynamic steal still pays for sentinel tiles that padding introduced; host valid-tile lists remain necessary.
Assuming SGD-shaped epilogues. The broadcast-Q dQ path is a many-to-one reduce-add into hot HBM addresses—profile it separately (Meta’s #1 backward gap).
Copying FA4 CuTe into Triton without warp roles. Without specialization and explicit TMEM lifetimes, you are back to the compiler-scheduled baseline.

title: PagedAttention and the KV Cache
text:
PagedAttention and the KV Cache
Autoregressive LLM serving is memory-bound in decode and capacity-bound in concurrency: each active sequence carries a growing key/value (KV) cache. Contiguous per-sequence KV allocations waste large fractions of GPU DRAM to fragmentation and over-reservation. PagedAttention (vLLM) borrows the OS virtual-memory idea—fixed-size blocks, a block table, allocate-on-demand—so attention kernels read logically contiguous tokens from physically non-contiguous KV blocks.
This chapter goes deeper than a one-paragraph mention in inference-serving notes: why contiguous KV fails, how block tables work, prefill vs decode implications, layout choices for custom kernels, and how to verify/benchmark paging behavior.

Attention still needs \(Q\) against all prior \(K\), and weighted sum over \(V\)—but the kernel gathers \(K,V\) through the block table instead of assuming one contiguous pointer.

title: PagedAttention and the KV Cache
text:
Why contiguous KV wastes memory
For a sequence with maximum length \(L_{\max}\) and current length \(t\):

Reservation waste: many systems allocate KV for \(L_{\max}\) up front even while \(t \ll L_{\max}\).

External fragmentation: variable-length contiguous regions cannot pack tightly as sequences finish at different times.

Batching rigidity: contiguous layouts make sharing prefixes or compacting live sequences expensive.

Empirical reports in the PagedAttention / vLLM line of work put waste often in the 60–80% range under contiguous reservation—memory that cannot become additional concurrent sequences. Paging caps internal waste at roughly one block (\(B\) tokens) per sequence (per managed cache partition) and removes most external fragmentation.

Capacity sketch
Let one token’s KV footprint (all layers, all heads, K and V) be \(b\) bytes. Contiguous reservation for \(N\) sequences costs \(\sim N L_{\max} b\). Paged on-demand costs \(\sim b\sum_i t_i\) plus \(< N B b\) partial-block slack (order-of-magnitude). The ratio \(L_{\max}/\bar{t}\) dominates the win when outputs are much shorter than the configured max.

title: PagedAttention and the KV Cache
text:
KV cache in Transformers (reminder)
For each layer \(\ell\) and head \(h\), token position \(i\) stores vectors \(k_i^{(\ell,h)}, v_i^{(\ell,h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\). Causality at decode step \(t\) uses
\[
\alpha_{t,i}=\mathrm{softmax}_i\left(\frac{q_t^\top k_i}{\sqrt{d}}\right),\qquad
o_t=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\alpha_{t,i}v_i.
\]
Prefill computes many \(q\) rows in parallel against the prompt’s \(K,V\); decode appends one new \((k_t,v_t)\) and attends with a single \(q_t\) (or a small speculative set).
Serving reality: weights are shared; KV grows per request. Throughput (tokens/s/GPU) often rises when more sequences fit—hence KV packing is a first-class systems problem, not a minor allocator tweak.

title: PagedAttention and the KV Cache
text:
Block structure
Choose block size \(B\) (vLLM commonly discusses values like 16). Logical block \(j\) holds tokens \((j-1)B+1,\ldots,jB\) (or \(0\)-based equivalents):
\[
K_j=(k_{(j-1)B+1},\ldots,k_{jB}),\qquad
V_j=(v_{(j-1)B+1},\ldots,v_{jB}).
\]
Attention becomes a loop over logical blocks: load the physical block pointed by the table, compute partial scores/outputs, advance. The last block carries a filled-token count \(1..B\).

Worked layout numbers
\(B=16\), head dim \(d=128\), dtype FP16: one head’s K block stores \(16\times 128\) elements \(=2048\) halves \(\approx 4\) KiB (order of magnitude), and V similarly. Multi-layer multi-head caches scale linearly; production engines may use separate block tables per layer/head partition or pack carefully for coalescing—design choice, not a change to the paging idea.

Allocate on demand: when decode would write past the filled count, pull a free physical block, append a table entry. Free on finish: return blocks to the pool (and decrement refcounts if shared).
decode step:

Prefix sharing (copy-on-write intuition)
If two requests share a prompt prefix, map their early logical blocks to the same physical blocks with elevated refcounts. Divergence (different generated tokens) allocates private blocks from the fork point. Automatic prefix caching builds on the same indirection: hash logical block contents (+prefix identity) to reuse physical KV.

Prefill vs decode under paging








Phase
Compute character
Paging interaction




Prefill
Compute-heavy; many tokens written
Allocate enough blocks for prompt; write K/V densely left-to-right; attention over prompt blocks


Decode
Memory-bound; one token at a time
Append into tail block; attention gathers all prior blocks for one \(q\)



Custom kernels must handle variable block lists per sequence in a batch: sequence A may have 3 blocks, sequence B 40. Batching strategies (continuous batching) reshape which sequences sit in a wave while the block tables remain the source of truth for KV addresses.

Implication
A FlashAttention-style tiled softmax over a contiguous \(K,V\) buffer is not drop-in compatible. You need a kernel that:

Accepts block tables + pool base pointers, or

Materializes contiguous KV (defeats paging), or

Uses a hybrid (e.g., paged decode kernels + specialized prefill paths).

vLLM’s historical PagedAttention CUDA kernels (attention_kernels-style designs) are built for case (1): thread blocks iterate paged K/V vectors with careful vectorized loads.

title: PagedAttention and the KV Cache
text:
Paged KV layouts (kernel writer view)
Exact layouts evolve; treat the following as a mental checklist when reading kernels or writing prototypes:
Pool: physical_block[p] → storage for B tokens × head_dim (K or V)

K access for logical token t:
  j = t / B
  o = t % B
  p = block_table[seq][j]
  addr = base_K + p * stride_block + o * stride_token + head_offset

V access: similar with base_V / possibly different vectorization shape
K vs V vectorization: kernels often pack K for efficient Q·K dots (e.g., threads cooperating on a head vector) while V layouts favor weighting and accumulating into the output. Do not assume K and V share identical lane mapping.
Separate K and V caches: common—two pools, parallel tables or mirrored indices.

Illustrative host-side table (not a production kernel)
# file: toy_block_table.py
# Toy model of logical→physical mapping (host-side). Not CUDA.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

B = 16


@dataclass
class SequenceKV:
    table: list[int] = field(default_factory=list)  # physical ids
    filled: int = 0  # tokens used in last block


class BlockPool:
    def __init__(self, n_blocks: int):
        self.free = list(range(n_blocks))

    def alloc(self) -> int:
        if not self.free:
            raise MemoryError("KV pool exhausted")
        return self.free.pop()

    def free_block(self, p: int) -> None:
        self.free.append(p)


def append_token(seq: SequenceKV, pool: BlockPool) -> None:
    if not seq.table or seq.filled == B:
        seq.table.append(pool.alloc())
        seq.filled = 0
    # device would write K/V into pool[seq.table[-1]][seq.filled]
    seq.filled += 1


def release(seq: SequenceKV, pool: BlockPool) -> None:
    for p in seq.table:
        pool.free_block(p)
    seq.table.clear()
    seq.filled = 0
Use this only to reason about allocation traffic; real engines track layers/heads, CUDA streams, and fragmentation across devices.

title: PagedAttention and the KV Cache
text:
Implications for custom kernels

Indirection tax: every K/V load pays a table lookup (often cached in shared memory / registers for the active block list).

Tail blocks: masks for filled < B are mandatory—same family of bugs as ragged sequence lengths.

Batching: one wave may include many tables; prefer grouped launches or paged-friendly attention APIs over naively padding to \(L_{\max}\) contiguous.

Fusion: paging composes with continuous batching, speculative decoding (extra parallel tokens), and quantization of KV (INT8/FP8 caches)—each changes strides and scales, not the block-table story.

Swap / multi-tier: physical blocks may live in CPU RAM; kernels and schedulers must not assume all table entries are GPU-resident without a residency check.

When generating kernels with AI assistants: specify block size, K/V separation, dtype, head dim, and tail masking explicitly. Ambiguous “write attention” prompts usually emit contiguous FlashAttention clones that cannot consume a paged pool.

title: Flash-Decoding: Split-KV Attention for Long-Context Decode
text:
Flash-Decoding: Split-KV Attention for Long-Context Decode
FlashAttention made prefill fast by tiling \(QK^\top\), softmax, and \(PV\) into one kernel that never writes the score matrix to HBM. Decode is a different problem. Each step has one new query row per sequence and head, attending over a KV cache that may hold tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens. A FlashAttention-style grid parallelizes over batch × heads × query tiles, and at decode there is only one query tile. With a small batch and a long context, that leaves a handful of CTAs to stream gigabytes of KV while most SMs sit idle.
Flash-Decoding (Dao, Haziza, Massa, Sizov, 2023) adds the missing parallel dimension: the KV sequence. Each split of the cache runs the familiar online-softmax loop independently and emits a partial output plus one scalar, its log-sum-exp (LSE). A tiny second kernel then merges the splits exactly. The authors reported up to 8× faster decode for very long sequences, and the same split-then-merge pattern now sits under paged decode kernels, cascade or shared-prefix attention, and context-parallel attention across GPUs.
This chapter builds the idea from the algebra up. It proves the merge is exact, writes a two-kernel Triton implementation that you can verify on a laptop with the Triton interpreter, compiles it for a GPU you do not own, ports the production split-count heuristic, and lists the checks that catch the real bugs.

title: Flash-Decoding: Split-KV Attention for Long-Context Decode
text:
1. Why decode starves the GPU
For one (sequence, head) pair at decode step \(t\):
\[
s_i=\frac{q^\top k_i}{\sqrt d},\qquad o=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\mathrm{softmax}(s)_i\,v_i .
\]
The work is about \(4td\) FLOPs against \(2td\) elements of K and V that must be read from HBM. In FP16 that is about 1 FLOP per byte, which puts it far left on the roofline: decode attention is purely bandwidth-bound. The only goal is to keep every SM’s load pipeline full.








Kernel style
Grid at decode
CTAs for batch 1, 8 KV heads




FlashAttention (one CTA per batch × head × query tile)
\(B\cdot H\cdot 1\)
8


Flash-Decoding (adds \(S\) KV splits)
\(B\cdot H\cdot S\)
\(8S\) (e.g. 232 with \(S=29\))




Worked numbers
Batch 1, 8 KV heads (grouped-query attention), context \(128\,000\), head dim 128, FP16 cache. K plus V for one layer is
\[
2\times 8\times 128\,000\times 128\times 2\ \text{B}\approx 524\ \text{MB}.
\]
At the H100 SXM’s roughly 3.35 TB/s HBM3 peak, that is about 160 µs per layer if bandwidth is saturated. Eight CTAs on a 132-SM part cannot get close: each SM can only keep a limited number of loads in flight. Splitting the sequence 29 ways gives 232 CTAs, enough to occupy every SM and keep loads outstanding. The model is the same and so are the bytes; the kernel is simply parallelized along the dimension that actually has work.
GQA note: with grouped-query attention, several query heads share one KV head. Good decode kernels pack the query heads of a group into the “M” rows of a tile (FlashAttention-3 calls this pack_gqa), so the KV block is loaded once per group, not once per query head. The parallelism problem, and the split-KV fix, are about KV heads × batch.

title: Flash-Decoding: Split-KV Attention for Long-Context Decode
section: 2. Mental model: attention states and the merge operator
text:
2. Mental model: attention states and the merge operator
For a set of key indices \(I\), define its attention state as the pair
\[
\mathrm{LSE}(I)=\log\sum_{i\in I}e^{s_i},\qquad
o(I)=\sum_{i\in I}\frac{e^{s_i}}{e^{\mathrm{LSE}(I)}}\,v_i .
\]
\(o(I)\) is the attention output you would get if the cache contained only the keys in \(I\). \(\mathrm{LSE}(I)\) records how much total softmax mass \(I\) carries.
Claim. For disjoint \(I\) and \(J\):
\[
\mathrm{LSE}(I\cup J)=\log\!\left(e^{\mathrm{LSE}(I)}+e^{\mathrm{LSE}(J)}\right),\qquad
o(I\cup J)=\frac{e^{\mathrm{LSE}(I)}\,o(I)+e^{\mathrm{LSE}(J)}\,o(J)}{e^{\mathrm{LSE}(I)}+e^{\mathrm{LSE}(J)}} .
\]
Proof. \(e^{\mathrm{LSE}(I)}\,o(I)=\sum_{i\in I}e^{s_i}v_i\) is the unnormalized numerator over \(I\), and \(e^{\mathrm{LSE}(I)}\) is the unnormalized denominator. Numerators and denominators over disjoint sets simply add. \(\blacksquare\)
Call this merge \(\oplus\). It is associative and commutative, so the splits can be combined in any order: sequentially, as a tree, across warps, across CTAs, or across GPUs. It is the same operator FlashAttention applies tile by tile inside one CTA (the online softmax), now applied between CTAs. FlashInfer makes it the canonical output of every attention kernel (“attention state”) and exposes merge_state / merge_states as first-class operations.
Numerically stable form. Never exponentiate an LSE directly. Subtract the maximum first:
\[
m=\max_j \mathrm{LSE}_j,\qquad w_j=e^{\mathrm{LSE}_j-m},\qquad o=\frac{\sum_j w_j\,o_j}{\sum_j w_j},\qquad \mathrm{LSE}=m+\log\sum_j w_j .
\]
            KV cache for one (sequence, head):  t tokens
 ┌───────────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┬──────────┐
 │   split 0     │   split 1     │   split 2     │ split 3  │   (last split may be short or empty)
 └──────┬────────┴──────┬────────┴──────┬────────┴────┬─────┘
        │ online softmax over BLOCK_N tiles (kernel 1, one CTA per split)
        ▼               ▼               ▼             ▼
   (o0, lse0)      (o1, lse1)      (o2, lse2)    (o3, lse3)     fp32 workspace in HBM
        └───────────────┴───────┬───────┴─────────────┘
                                ▼  kernel 2: m = max lse; w = exp(lse - m); o = Σ w·o / Σ w
                         final o  (and lse, if a caller wants to merge further)

title: Flash-Decoding: Split-KV Attention for Long-Context Decode
section: 3. Verify the algebra before writing a kernel
text:
3. Verify the algebra before writing a kernel
Start with a host reference so that every GPU result later has a ground truth.
# file: split_kv_reference.py
# NumPy reference: one decode query against a long KV cache, computed
#  (a) in one pass, and (b) as Flash-Decoding style splits merged by log-sum-exp.
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
D, T, S = 128, 10_000, 7            # head dim, cached tokens, number of KV splits
q = rng.standard_normal(D).astype(np.float32)
K = rng.standard_normal((T, D)).astype(np.float32)
V = rng.standard_normal((T, D)).astype(np.float32)
scale = 1.0 / np.sqrt(D)


def attend(q, K, V):
    """Return (o, lse) for one query over a KV segment: o normalised, lse = log sum exp(s)."""
    s = (K @ q) * scale
    m = s.max()
    p = np.exp(s - m)
    l = p.sum()
    return (p @ V) / l, m + np.log(l)


def merge(states):
    """Combine (o_i, lse_i) partial states into the exact full-segment state."""
    lse = np.array([st[1] for st in states])
    m = lse.max()
    w = np.exp(lse - m)                    # unnormalised weight of each split
    o = sum(wi * st[0] for wi, st in zip(w, states)) / w.sum()
    return o, m + np.log(w.sum())


o_full, lse_full = attend(q, K, V)

bounds = np.linspace(0, T, S + 1).astype(int)          # uneven split lengths are fine
parts = [attend(q, K[a:b], V[a:b]) for a, b in zip(bounds[:-1], bounds[1:])]
o_split, lse_split = merge(parts)

# The merge is associative: merging pairwise in a tree gives the same answer.
tree = merge([merge(parts[:3]), merge(parts[3:])])

print("split boundaries :", bounds.tolist())
print("max |o_full - o_split| =", float(np.abs(o_full - o_split).max()))
print("|lse_full - lse_split| =", float(abs(lse_full - lse_split)))
print("max |o_split - o_tree|  =", float(np.abs(o_split - tree[0]).max()))

|lse_full - lse_split| = 1.7920598338605487e-10
max |o_split - o_tree|  = 1.3877787807814457e-17
Split, merge, or tree-merge: the results agree to rounding. Uneven split lengths do not matter, because each split’s LSE carries its own weight.

The trap: the textbook merge overflows
# file: merge_trap.py
# The textbook merge  o = sum(exp(lse_i) * o_i) / sum(exp(lse_i))  overflows float32
# as soon as any lse_i > ~88.7. Subtracting max(lse) first is not optional.
import numpy as np

lse = np.array([95.0, 97.5, 91.2], dtype=np.float32)        # plausible with large logits
o = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [0.5, 0.5]], dtype=np.float32)

with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    w_naive = np.exp(lse)
    print("naive weights :", w_naive)
    print("naive merge   :", (w_naive[:, None] * o).sum(0) / w_naive.sum())

m = lse.max()
w = np.exp(lse - m)
print("stable weights:", w)
print("stable merge  :", (w[:, None] * o).sum(0) / w.sum())
print("merged lse    :", m + np.log(w.sum()))

naive weights : [inf inf inf]
naive merge   : [nan nan]
stable weights: [0.08208501 1.         0.0018363 ]
stable merge  : [0.07657673 0.92342323]

exp overflows FP32 above about 88.7, and LSE values that large are routine once logits grow (long contexts, no QK-norm, large activations). Kernels that “pass the unit test” with randn inputs and then NaN in production usually have exactly this bug in the combine step.

title: Flash-Decoding: Split-KV Attention for Long-Context Decode
text:
4. A two-kernel Triton implementation
The design is the minimum that is still honest about production concerns:

Kernel 1 (split_kv_kernel), grid \((B\cdot H,\ S)\). Each program owns one split of one (sequence, head) pair, streams its keys in BLOCK_N tiles with the online-softmax recurrence, and writes a normalized partial output and its LSE to an FP32 workspace.
Kernel 2 (combine_kernel), grid \((B\cdot H)\). Loads \(S\) LSEs and \(S\) partial outputs, applies the stable merge, and writes the result.
Ragged batches. SEQ_LENS[b] bounds every sequence, so a sequence shorter than the split layout leaves some splits empty. An empty split must write \(o=0\) and \(\mathrm{LSE}=-\infty\), giving it weight \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Writing \(0/0\) there is the classic NaN.
FP32 everywhere it matters. Scores, running max, running sum, accumulator, and workspace are all FP32, whatever the cache dtype. FlashAttention-2’s split-KV path allocates its out_accum and softmax_lse_accum workspaces in FP32 for the same reason.

# file: flash_decode_triton.py
# Two-kernel Flash-Decoding (split-KV) for batched single-token decode, written in Triton.
#   kernel 1: grid = (batch*heads, num_splits)  -> partial (o, lse) per split
#   kernel 2: grid = (batch*heads,)             -> log-sum-exp merge across splits
# Runs on a GPU, or on CPU for correctness work with:  TRITON_INTERPRET=1 python flash_decode_triton.py
import math
import os

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def split_kv_kernel(Q, K, V, SEQ_LENS, O_PART, LSE_PART,
                    stride_kb, stride_kh, stride_kt,      # K/V: [B, H, T_max, D], last dim contiguous
                    H, chunk, scale,
                    D: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr, NUM_SPLITS: tl.constexpr):
    bh = tl.program_id(0)
    split = tl.program_id(1)
    b = bh // H
    h = bh % H
    seq_len = tl.load(SEQ_LENS + b)

    start = split * chunk
    end = tl.minimum(start + chunk, seq_len)               # may be <= start: empty split

    offs_d = tl.arange(0, D)
    q = tl.load(Q + bh * D + offs_d).to(tl.float32)        # Q: [B*H, D]
    kv_base = b * stride_kb + h * stride_kh

    m_i = -float("inf")                                    # running max of scores
    l_i = 0.0                                              # running sum of exp(score - m_i)
    acc = tl.zeros([D], dtype=tl.float32)                  # running sum of p * v

    for n0 in range(start, end, BLOCK_N):
        offs_n = n0 + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N)
        mask_n = offs_n < end
        ptrs = kv_base + offs_n[:, None] * stride_kt + offs_d[None, :]
        k = tl.load(K + ptrs, mask=mask_n[:, None], other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
        s = tl.sum(k * q[None, :], axis=1) * scale         # [BLOCK_N] scores
        s = tl.where(mask_n, s, -float("inf"))
        m_new = tl.maximum(m_i, tl.max(s, axis=0))
        alpha = tl.exp(m_i - m_new)                        # rescale old state
        p = tl.exp(s - m_new)
        v = tl.load(V + ptrs, mask=mask_n[:, None], other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
        acc = acc * alpha + tl.sum(p[:, None] * v, axis=0)
        l_i = l_i * alpha + tl.sum(p, axis=0)
        m_i = m_new

    has_keys = end > start
    safe_l = tl.where(has_keys, l_i, 1.0)
    o = tl.where(has_keys, acc / safe_l, 0.0)              # empty split -> o = 0 ...
    lse = tl.where(has_keys, m_i + tl.log(safe_l), -float("inf"))  # ... with weight exp(-inf) = 0
    out = bh * NUM_SPLITS + split
    tl.store(O_PART + out * D + offs_d, o)
    tl.store(LSE_PART + out, lse)


@triton.jit
def combine_kernel(O_PART, LSE_PART, O,
                   D: tl.constexpr, NUM_SPLITS: tl.constexpr):
    bh = tl.program_id(0)
    offs_s = tl.arange(0, NUM_SPLITS)
    offs_d = tl.arange(0, D)
    lse = tl.load(LSE_PART + bh * NUM_SPLITS + offs_s)      # [S]
    m = tl.max(lse, axis=0)
    w = tl.exp(lse - m)                                     # empty splits contribute 0
    o_part = tl.load(O_PART + (bh * NUM_SPLITS + offs_s)[:, None] * D + offs_d[None, :])
    o = tl.sum(w[:, None] * o_part, axis=0) / tl.sum(w, axis=0)
    tl.store(O + bh * D + offs_d, o)


def flash_decode(q, k, v, seq_lens, num_splits=8, block_n=32):
    """q: [B, H, D]; k, v: [B, H, T_max, D]; seq_lens: [B] int32. Returns [B, H, D] float32."""
    B, H, T_max, D = k.shape
    chunk = triton.cdiv(T_max, num_splits)
    o_part = torch.empty(B * H, num_splits, D, dtype=torch.float32, device=q.device)
    lse_part = torch.empty(B * H, num_splits, dtype=torch.float32, device=q.device)
    out = torch.empty(B, H, D, dtype=torch.float32, device=q.device)
    split_kv_kernel[(B * H, num_splits)](
        q.contiguous(), k, v, seq_lens, o_part, lse_part,
        k.stride(0), k.stride(1), k.stride(2),
        H, chunk, 1.0 / math.sqrt(D),
        D=D, BLOCK_N=block_n, NUM_SPLITS=num_splits)
    combine_kernel[(B * H,)](o_part, lse_part, out, D=D, NUM_SPLITS=num_splits)
    return out


def reference(q, k, v, seq_lens):
    B, H, _, D = k.shape
    out = torch.empty(B, H, D, dtype=torch.float32)
    for b in range(B):
        L = int(seq_lens[b])
        s = torch.einsum("hd,htd->ht", q[b].float(), k[b, :, :L].float()) / math.sqrt(D)
        out[b] = torch.einsum("ht,htd->hd", torch.softmax(s, dim=-1), v[b, :, :L].float())
    return out


if __name__ == "__main__":
    device = "cpu" if os.environ.get("TRITON_INTERPRET") == "1" else "cuda"
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    B, H, T_max, D = 3, 4, 1000, 64
    seq_lens = torch.tensor([1000, 37, 1], dtype=torch.int32, device=device)  # ragged batch
    q = torch.randn(B, H, D, device=device)
    k = torch.randn(B, H, T_max, D, device=device)
    v = torch.randn(B, H, T_max, D, device=device)
    for q_gain in (1.0, 40.0):                        # 40x -> logits in the hundreds
        for splits in (1, 4, 8):
            qq = q * q_gain
            got = flash_decode(qq, k, v, seq_lens, num_splits=splits)
            ref = reference(qq.cpu(), k.cpu(), v.cpu(), seq_lens.cpu())
            err = (got.cpu() - ref).abs().max().item()
            print(f"q_gain={q_gain:>4}  num_splits={splits}:  max abs error = {err:.2e}")

5. Compile for a GPU you do not have
Interpreter success does not guarantee that the kernel lowers. Loop-carried values that change dtype, non-constexpr shapes, and unsupported ops fail only in the real compiler. Triton can compile ahead of time for a named target on a CPU-only machine:
# file: compile_check.py
# Ahead-of-time compile both kernels for an H100 (sm_90) on a machine with no GPU.
# Catches type errors, bad constexpr use and loop-carried dtype mismatches before you rent a GPU.
import triton
from triton.backends.compiler import GPUTarget
from triton.compiler import ASTSource

from flash_decode_triton import combine_kernel, split_kv_kernel

target = GPUTarget("cuda", 90, 32)          # backend, compute capability, warp size
split_sig = {"Q": "*fp32", "K": "*fp32", "V": "*fp32", "SEQ_LENS": "*i32",
             "O_PART": "*fp32", "LSE_PART": "*fp32",
             "stride_kb": "i32", "stride_kh": "i32", "stride_kt": "i32",
             "H": "i32", "chunk": "i32", "scale": "fp32",
             "D": "constexpr", "BLOCK_N": "constexpr", "NUM_SPLITS": "constexpr"}
combine_sig = {"O_PART": "*fp32", "LSE_PART": "*fp32", "O": "*fp32",
               "D": "constexpr", "NUM_SPLITS": "constexpr"}

jobs = [
    ("split_kv_kernel", ASTSource(fn=split_kv_kernel, signature=split_sig,
                                  constexprs={"D": 128, "BLOCK_N": 64, "NUM_SPLITS": 32})),
    ("combine_kernel", ASTSource(fn=combine_kernel, signature=combine_sig,
                                 constexprs={"D": 128, "NUM_SPLITS": 32})),
]
for name, src in jobs:
    k = triton.compile(src, target=target)
    md = k.metadata
    print(f"{name:16s} stages={','.join(k.asm.keys())}  "
          f"num_warps={md.num_warps}  shared={md.shared} B  ptx_lines={k.asm['ptx'].count(chr(10))}")

combine_kernel   stages=source,ttir,ttgir,llir,ptx,cubin  num_warps=4  shared=0 B  ptx_lines=1035

In this build every K/V load comes out as a scalar ld.global.b32, because the hand-written signature tells the compiler nothing about pointer alignment or stride divisibility. At a normal launch, Triton specializes on arguments that are divisible by 16, and that specialization is what typically unlocks wider vector loads. Grepping the PTX of the kernel you actually launch is a cheap way to confirm you got them.
Wire this compile check, together with the interpreter test, into the agent loop as a cheap gate before any GPU time is spent.

6. How many splits?
Too few splits leave SMs idle. Too many add workspace traffic and combine work, and make each split too short to amortize its prologue. FlashAttention-2’s dispatcher chooses \(S\) by wave efficiency: launch \(B\cdot H\cdot S\) CTAs onto a fixed number of slots, and prefer the smallest \(S\) whose last wave is nearly as full as the best achievable.
# file: choose_splits.py
# Wave-efficiency heuristic for picking the number of KV splits, ported from the
# FlashAttention-2 split-KV dispatcher (num_splits_heuristic in csrc/flash_attn/flash_api.cpp).
import math


def num_splits(work_items, slots, n_kv_blocks, max_splits=128):
    if work_items >= 0.8 * slots:           # already ~fills the machine: do not split
        return 1
    max_splits = min(max_splits, slots, n_kv_blocks)

    def eligible(s):                        # 11 vs 12 splits of 64 blocks is really 11 splits
        return s == 1 or math.ceil(n_kv_blocks / s) != math.ceil(n_kv_blocks / (s - 1))

    eff = {}
    for s in range(1, max_splits + 1):
        if eligible(s):
            waves = work_items * s / slots
            eff[s] = waves / math.ceil(waves)   # fraction of the last wave that is busy
    best = max(eff.values())
    return next(s for s in sorted(eff) if eff[s] >= 0.85 * best)


SMS = 132                    # e.g. H100 SXM; FA2 passes 2 * num_SMs as the slot count
BLOCK_N = 128                # KV tokens per inner tile for head_dim 128
print(f"{'batch':>5} {'heads':>8} {'context':>8} {'work':>5} {'splits':>6} {'CTAs':>5}")
for batch, heads, ctx in [(1, 8, 128_000), (1, 32, 32_000), (4, 8, 8_000),
                          (16, 8, 4_000), (64, 32, 2_000), (1, 8, 300)]:
    work = batch * heads
    s = num_splits(work, 2 * SMS, math.ceil(ctx / BLOCK_N))
    print(f"{batch:>5} {heads:>8} {ctx:>8} {work:>5} {s:>6} {work * s:>5}")

batch    heads  context  work splits  CTAs

    4        8     8000    32      7   224

    1        8      300     8      3    24
Reading the table:

Small batch, long context is where Flash-Decoding matters: 8 work items become 232 CTAs.
Large batch already fills the machine (2048 work items), so the heuristic returns 1 split and the extra pass is skipped entirely.
Short context is capped by the number of KV tiles: 300 tokens are only 3 tiles of 128, so at most 3 splits.
The “eligible” check skips split counts that produce the same tiles per split as a smaller count, which would add a combine for nothing.

Overhead check. Per (sequence, head), the workspace costs \(S\cdot d\) FP32 values written and read back, about \(8Sd\) bytes, while the KV stream is \(4td\) bytes in FP16. The ratio \(2S/t\) is about \(0.05\%\) for \(S=29\), \(t=128\,000\). The combine kernel should be a sliver in an Nsight Systems timeline. If it is not, \(S\) is too large or the combine is badly written.

title: TurboQuant: Rotate-then-Quantize KV Caches at 3 Bits
text:
TurboQuant: Rotate-then-Quantize KV Caches at 3 Bits
Long-context decode is a bandwidth problem that turns into a capacity problem. Every generated token reads the whole KV cache of its sequence, and every concurrent sequence keeps its own cache in HBM. FP8 caches halve the bill. Going below 8 bits is harder: keys carry outlier channels, a handful of dimensions whose magnitude is ten or twenty times the rest, and a naive 3-bit quantizer spends all its levels on them.
TurboQuant (Zandieh, Daliri, Hadian, Mirrokni; arXiv April 2025, ICLR 2026) handles outliers by changing the basis instead of fighting them. Multiply each vector by a random orthogonal matrix and every coordinate starts to look like a draw from one known distribution, the same for every vector and every channel. A single precomputed scalar codebook is then close to optimal everywhere. You store a few bits per coordinate and one norm per vector, with no per-block scales or zero points and no calibration data.
This chapter builds the quantizer in NumPy and checks the paper’s distortion numbers. It also shows the result that decides how TurboQuant gets deployed: the unbiased inner-product variant (with QJL) loses to the plain MSE variant inside softmax attention. After that come the kernel-side algebra that makes decode cheap, where the method runs in production today, and the prior-art dispute around it.
Everything here runs on a CPU. The listings were run on Debian 13.7 with Python 3.13.5, NumPy 2.5.3 and SciPy 1.18.1, and the outputs are pasted unedited. GPU throughput numbers are quoted from their sources and labeled as such.

section: 1. Why the KV cache is the thing to compress
text:
1. Why the KV cache is the thing to compress
For a GQA model, each token stores one key and one value vector per KV head per layer:
\[\text{bytes/token} = 2 \cdot L \cdot H_{kv} \cdot d \cdot \tfrac{b}{8}.\]
Weights are a fixed cost. The KV cache grows with context length times batch size, and decode reads all of it for every token. Compressing it buys capacity (more sequences or longer contexts) and bandwidth (fewer bytes per decode step) at once.
# file: kv_budget.py
# KV-cache bytes per token, and what a bit budget buys, for two GQA models.
GiB = 1024**3

models = {  # name: (layers, kv_heads, head_dim)
    "Llama-3.1-8B": (32, 8, 128),
    "Llama-3.1-70B": (80, 8, 128),
}

def kv_bytes_per_token(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, bits_per_coord, overhead_bits_per_vec=0):
    vectors = 2 * layers * kv_heads                     # one K and one V per head per layer
    return vectors * (head_dim * bits_per_coord + overhead_bits_per_vec) / 8

budget = 40 * GiB  # memory left for KV after weights, say
print(f"{'model':14} {'format':26} {'KiB/token':>9} {'x vs bf16':>9} {'tokens in 40 GiB':>17}")
for name, (L, H, d) in models.items():

    for label, bits, ovh in [("bf16", 16, 0),
                             ("fp8", 8, 0),

                             ("3.5-bit + fp16 norm", 3.5, 16),
                             ("3-bit + fp16 norm", 3, 16),
                             ("2.5-bit + fp16 norm", 2.5, 16)]:

title: TurboQuant: Rotate-then-Quantize KV Caches at 3 Bits
section: 2. Mental model: make every coordinate look the same, then use one codebook
text:
2. Mental model: make every coordinate look the same, then use one codebook
 key k (d=128, outlier channels)        rotated  y = Π k/||k||           stored
 ┌─────────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐
 │ ▁▁█▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▆▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▇▁▁▁▁ │  Π    │ ▃▄▂▅▃▂▄▃▅▂▃▄▂▃▅▄▂▃▄▃▂▅▃▄▂▃ │ Q │ idx: b bits × d  │
 │ few huge channels, rest tiny│ ────► │ every coord ≈ N(0, 1/d)     │──►│ ||k||: one fp16  │
 └─────────────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────┘
 dequant:  k̂ = ||k|| · Πᵀ c[idx]          c = Lloyd-Max centroids for N(0,1/d), fixed per (d, b)
Three facts carry the method.

A random rotation spreads energy. If \(\Pi\) is a uniformly random orthogonal matrix and \(u\) a unit vector, \(\Pi u\) is uniform on the sphere \(S^{d-1}\), whatever \(u\) was. One coordinate of a uniform point on the sphere has density proportional to \((1-x^2)^{(d-3)/2}\) on \([-1, 1]\), which is very close to \(\mathcal N(0, 1/d)\) for \(d \ge 64\). The outliers are gone, smeared across all 128 coordinates.
In high dimension the coordinates are nearly independent. That makes per-coordinate scalar quantization nearly as good as vector quantization. The paper proves the MSE quantizer’s distortion is within a factor \(\sqrt{3}\pi/2 \approx 2.7\) of the information-theoretic lower bound \(4^{-b}\) for every input, and much closer at low bit-widths.
The codebook is data-independent. The distribution in (1) depends only on \(d\), so the optimal \(2^b\) levels (Lloyd-Max for that density) are computed once, offline. Nothing is learned from the model, and quantization is online: one vector in, one code out, so it works token by token during decode.

A dense Haar rotation costs \(O(d^2)\) per vector. Production code uses a randomized Hadamard transform \(y = H D x\) (\(D\) a random \(\pm 1\) diagonal, \(H\) the orthonormal Walsh–Hadamard matrix). It costs \(O(d \log d)\), is exactly orthogonal, and is close enough to Haar for this purpose. Section 8 shows what happens when you drop \(D\).

title: TurboQuant: Rotate-then-Quantize KV Caches at 3 Bits
text:
3. The quantizer in NumPy
tq_core.py contains everything: the Hadamard butterfly, the two rotations, the Lloyd-Max solver for the sphere-coordinate density, the MSE quantizer, and the inner-product quantizer that adds a 1-bit QJL sketch of the residual.
# file: tq_core.py
# The pieces of a TurboQuant-style vector quantizer, in plain NumPy:
#   randomized Hadamard rotation, a Lloyd-Max codebook for the coordinates of a
#   random unit vector, the MSE quantizer, and the QJL residual sketch.
import numpy as np


def fwht(x):
    """Orthonormal fast Walsh-Hadamard transform along the last axis (length 2^m)."""
    x = np.array(x, dtype=np.float64, copy=True)
    shape, n = x.shape, x.shape[-1]
    assert n & (n - 1) == 0, "Hadamard length must be a power of two"
    x = x.reshape(-1, n)
    h = 1
    while h < n:
        x = x.reshape(-1, n // (2 * h), 2, h)
        a = x[:, :, 0, :].copy()
        b = x[:, :, 1, :]
        x[:, :, 0, :] = a + b
        x[:, :, 1, :] = a - b
        x = x.reshape(-1, n)
        h *= 2
    return x.reshape(shape) / np.sqrt(n)


class RandomizedHadamard:
    """y = H D x with D a fixed random +-1 diagonal. Orthogonal, O(d log d), and its own
    transpose up to D: x = D H y."""

    def __init__(self, d, rng):
        self.signs = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=d)

    def forward(self, x):
        return fwht(x * self.signs)

    def inverse(self, y):
        return fwht(y) * self.signs


def lloyd_max_sphere(d, bits, grid=400_001, iters=300):
    """Optimal scalar codebook for one coordinate of a uniform random unit vector in R^d.
    That coordinate has density proportional to (1 - x^2)^((d - 3) / 2) on [-1, 1]."""
    x = np.linspace(-1, 1, grid)
    w = np.clip(1 - x * x, 0, None) ** ((d - 3) / 2)
    w /= w.sum()
    k = 2**bits
    sd = 1 / np.sqrt(d)
    c = np.linspace(-2 * sd, 2 * sd, k)                  # start near the bulk of the mass
    for _ in range(iters):
        edges = (c[1:] + c[:-1]) / 2                     # nearest-centroid boundaries
        cell = np.searchsorted(edges, x)
        mass = np.bincount(cell, weights=w, minlength=k)
        c = np.bincount(cell, weights=w * x, minlength=k) / mass   # centroid = conditional mean
    edges = (c[1:] + c[:-1]) / 2
    mse_per_coord = np.sum(w * (x - c[np.searchsorted(edges, x)]) ** 2)
    return c, edges, d * mse_per_coord                  # last value: E||u - Q(u)||^2 for unit u


class HaarRotation:
    """A dense uniformly random orthogonal matrix (QR of a Gaussian, signs fixed). O(d^2)."""

    def __init__(self, d, rng):
        q, r = np.linalg.qr(rng.standard_normal((d, d)))
        self.Q = q * np.sign(np.diag(r))

    def forward(self, x):
        return x @ self.Q.T

    def inverse(self, y):
        return y @ self.Q


class TurboQuantMSE:
    """Store b-bit indices per coordinate plus one norm per vector."""

    def __init__(self, d, bits, rng, norm_correction=False, rotation=RandomizedHadamard):
        self.rot = rotation(d, rng)
        self.centroids, self.edges, self.theory_mse = lloyd_max_sphere(d, bits)
        self.norm_correction = norm_correction

    def quantize(self, x):
        norm = np.linalg.norm(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
        y = self.rot.forward(x / norm)
        return np.searchsorted(self.edges, y).astype(np.uint8), norm.astype(np.float16)

    def dequantize(self, idx, norm):
        y = self.centroids[idx]
        if self.norm_correction:                         # put the codeword back on the sphere
            y = y / np.linalg.norm(y, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
        return norm.astype(np.float64) * self.rot.inverse(y)


class TurboQuantProd:
    """(b-1)-bit MSE quantizer, then a 1-bit QJL sketch of the residual: an unbiased
    estimator of inner products <q, x>."""

    def __init__(self, d, bits, rng):
        self.mse = TurboQuantMSE(d, bits - 1, rng)
        self.S = rng.standard_normal((d, d))
        self.d = d

    def quantize(self, x):
        idx, norm = self.mse.quantize(x)
        r = x - self.mse.dequantize(idx, norm)
        return idx, norm, np.sign(r @ self.S.T).astype(np.int8), np.linalg.norm(r, axis=-1, keepdims=True)

    def dequantize(self, idx, norm, qjl, rnorm):
        corr = np.sqrt(np.pi / 2) / self.d * rnorm * (qjl @ self.S)
        return self.mse.dequantize(idx, norm) + corr
A few details matter:

Normalize, then rotate. The codebook is designed for coordinates of a unit vector. Storing \(\lVert x \rVert\) separately is what lets one codebook serve every token. (vLLM stores it as fp16.)
Indices are searched against midpoints. With sorted centroids, nearest-centroid assignment is a binary search over \(2^b - 1\) boundaries. vLLM’s Triton store kernel does exactly that.
norm_correction rescales the decoded codeword back to unit length before un-rotating. Quantization shrinks vectors (the centroids are conditional means, which sit inside the sphere), and the correction undoes that radial bias. vLLM’s _nc presets turn it on, and its docs report about 0.8% perplexity gain at 4 bits.
QJL (Zandieh, Daliri, Han; AAAI 2025) stores \(\operatorname{sign}(S r)\) for a Gaussian matrix \(S\) and the residual \(r\), plus \(\lVert r \rVert\). The estimator \(\sqrt{\pi/2}\,/\,d \cdot \lVert r\rVert\, S^\top \operatorname{sign}(S r)\) is unbiased for inner products with \(r\). Spending one of the \(b\) bits on it makes \(\langle q, \hat x\rangle\) unbiased.

# file: tq_codebook.py
# Lloyd-Max codebooks for the coordinates of a random unit vector, and the distortion
# they buy, next to the numbers in the TurboQuant paper and its upper/lower bounds.
import numpy as np

from tq_core import HaarRotation, RandomizedHadamard, TurboQuantMSE, lloyd_max_sphere

paper = {1: 0.36, 2: 0.117, 3: 0.03, 4: 0.009}

    print(f"{b:>4} {D:12.4f} {paper[b]:6.3f} {4.0**-b:10.4f} {np.sqrt(3) * np.pi / 2 * 4.0**-b:23.4f}")

for b in (2, 3):
    for rot in (HaarRotation, RandomizedHadamard):
        tq = TurboQuantMSE(d, b, rng, rotation=rot)
        res = []
        for x in (iso, spiky):
            xh = tq.dequantize(*tq.quantize(x))
            res.append(np.mean(np.sum((x - xh) ** 2, 1) / np.sum(x**2, 1)))
        print(f"{b}-bit {rot.__name__:18} isotropic {res[0]:.4f}  spiky {res[1]:.4f}  "

title: TurboQuant: Rotate-then-Quantize KV Caches at 3 Bits
text:
5. Against the obvious 3-bit baselines
The comparison that matters for attention is the error in the logits \(q \cdot k / \sqrt d\), not reconstruction MSE. This listing builds keys with four hot channels and a per-channel offset (the pattern KIVI and KVQuant reported in real K caches), plus queries that lean on the same channels, and tries six 3-bit schemes.
# file: tq_vs_naive.py
# 3-bit keys with channel outliers: naive per-token scaling vs per-channel scaling
# vs rotate-then-quantize. Error measured on the keys and on attention logits q.k/sqrt(d).
import numpy as np

from tq_core import RandomizedHadamard, TurboQuantMSE

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n, d, bits = 4096, 128, 3
scale = np.ones(d)
scale[[3, 17, 64, 101]] = [18.0, 12.0, 9.0, 15.0]    # a few hot channels, same for every token
K = rng.standard_normal((n, d)) * scale + 0.5 * scale  # plus a per-channel offset
Q = rng.standard_normal((64, d)) * np.sqrt(scale)      # queries lean on the same channels


def uniform_absmax(x, bits, axis):
    """Symmetric round-to-nearest with one fp16 scale per slice along `axis`."""
    qmax = 2 ** (bits - 1) - 1
    s = np.abs(x).max(axis=axis, keepdims=True) / qmax
    return np.clip(np.round(x / s), -qmax - 1, qmax) * s


def uniform_minmax(x, bits, axis):
    """Asymmetric round-to-nearest with fp16 scale and zero point per slice."""
    lo, hi = x.min(axis=axis, keepdims=True), x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    s = (hi - lo) / (2**bits - 1)
    return np.round((x - lo) / s) * s + lo


rht = RandomizedHadamard(d, rng)
tq = TurboQuantMSE(d, bits, rng)
tq_nc = TurboQuantMSE(d, bits, rng, norm_correction=True)
schemes = {
    "per-token absmax": uniform_absmax(K, bits, axis=1),
    "per-token min-max": uniform_minmax(K, bits, axis=1),
    "per-channel min-max": uniform_minmax(K, bits, axis=0),
    "RHT + per-token min-max": rht.inverse(uniform_minmax(rht.forward(K), bits, axis=1)),
    "TurboQuant-MSE": tq.dequantize(*tq.quantize(K)),
    "TurboQuant-MSE + norm fix": tq_nc.dequantize(*tq_nc.quantize(K)),
}
L = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)
print(f"n={n} keys, d={d}, {bits} bits/coord, logit std {L.std():.2f}")
print(f"{'scheme':27} {'key rel. MSE':>12} {'logit RMSE':>10} {'top-1 match':>11}")
for name, Kh in schemes.items():
    rel = np.sum((K - Kh) ** 2) / np.sum(K**2)
    Lh = Q @ Kh.T / np.sqrt(d)
    top1 = np.mean(L.argmax(1) == Lh.argmax(1))
    print(f"{name:27} {rel:12.4f} {np.sqrt(np.mean((L - Lh) ** 2)):10.3f} {top1:11.2%}")

per-token min-max                 0.2198      1.488      54.69%

Three lessons:

Per-token scaling fails on outlier channels. The scale is set by the hottest channel, so the 120 ordinary channels round to one or two levels.
Per-channel scaling wins on key MSE and loses on logits. Per-channel scaling (what KIVI does for keys) spreads the absolute error evenly. The hot channels have huge ranges, so their absolute error is large, and those are exactly the channels the queries weight. Reconstruction MSE is the wrong metric.
The rotation does most of the work. At 3 bits, a randomized Hadamard followed by a plain per-token min-max quantizer is already within noise of TurboQuant-MSE. The Lloyd-Max codebook and norm storage add a little accuracy and remove the per-token scale and zero point (one fp16 instead of two). The top-1 column is computed over 64 queries, so treat differences of a few percent as noise.

title: TurboQuant: Rotate-then-Quantize KV Caches at 3 Bits
section: 6. The trap: unbiased is not the same as better
text:
6. The trap: unbiased is not the same as better
The paper offers two quantizers. TurboQuant-MSE minimizes \(\lVert x - \hat x\rVert^2\). TurboQuant-prod spends one bit on QJL so that \(\mathbb E\,\langle q, \hat x\rangle = \langle q, x\rangle\) exactly. Inner products are what attention computes, so the unbiased one looks like the right choice for keys. Check it against softmax.
# file: tq_prod.py
# Biased-but-tight (MSE) vs unbiased-but-noisy (MSE + QJL) inner products, and what
# each does to a peaked softmax over 4096 keys.
import numpy as np

from tq_core import TurboQuantMSE, TurboQuantProd

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
d, n = 128, 4096

# Part 1: <q, k^> against <q, k> for unit vectors. Slope 1 = unbiased.
k = rng.standard_normal((n, d))
k /= np.linalg.norm(k, axis=1, keepdims=True)
q = k[:512] + 0.6 * rng.standard_normal((512, d)) / np.sqrt(d)   # queries correlated with keys
q /= np.linalg.norm(q, axis=1, keepdims=True)
true = np.sum(q * k[:512], 1)
print("inner products, 512 correlated (q, k) pairs")
print(f"{'quantizer':22} {'slope':>6} {'resid std':>9}")
for bits in (2, 3, 4):
    for name, tq in ((f"MSE {bits}-bit", TurboQuantMSE(d, bits, rng)),
                     (f"MSE {bits - 1}-bit + QJL", TurboQuantProd(d, bits, rng))):
        est = np.sum(q * tq.dequantize(*tq.quantize(k[:512])), 1)
        slope = np.dot(est, true) / np.dot(true, true)
        print(f"{name:22} {slope:6.3f} {np.std(est - slope * true):9.4f}")

# Part 2: attention with one relevant key (logit ~ 9 above the crowd).
print("\nattention, 3 bits per key coordinate, 200 trials")
print(f"{'keys':18} {'p(needle)':>9} {'TV distance':>11} {'output rel err':>14}")
quants = {"fp32": None, "MSE 3-bit": TurboQuantMSE(d, 3, rng),
          "MSE 2-bit + QJL": TurboQuantProd(d, 3, rng)}
stats = {name: [] for name in quants}
for t in range(200):
    K = rng.standard_normal((n, d))
    V = rng.standard_normal((n, d))
    qv = rng.standard_normal(d)
    K[7] = 9.0 * np.sqrt(d) * qv / (qv @ qv) + 0.3 * K[7]       # the needle: logit ~ 9
    p_ref = None
    for name, tq in quants.items():
        Kh = K if tq is None else tq.dequantize(*tq.quantize(K))
        logits = Kh @ qv / np.sqrt(d)
        p = np.exp(logits - logits.max())
        p /= p.sum()
        if p_ref is None:
            p_ref, o_ref = p, p @ V
        o = p @ V
        stats[name].append((p[7], 0.5 * np.abs(p - p_ref).sum(),
                            np.linalg.norm(o - o_ref) / np.linalg.norm(o_ref)))
for name, rows in stats.items():
    m = np.mean(rows, axis=0)
    print(f"{name:18} {m[0]:9.3f} {m[1]:11.3f} {m[2]:14.3f}")

quantizer               slope resid std
MSE 2-bit               0.883    0.0331
MSE 1-bit + QJL         1.003    0.0620
MSE 3-bit               0.967    0.0231
MSE 2-bit + QJL         1.001    0.0355
MSE 4-bit               0.991    0.0125
MSE 3-bit + QJL         1.001    0.0200

attention, 3 bits per key coordinate, 200 trials
keys               p(needle) TV distance output rel err
fp32                   0.534       0.000          0.000
MSE 3-bit              0.473       0.081          0.123
MSE 2-bit + QJL        0.509       0.118          0.126
Part 1 shows the trade:

MSE quantizers shrink inner products. The slope is 0.88 at 2 bits and 0.97 at 3 bits, the same radial shrinkage that norm_correction fixes. At 1 bit the shrinkage is exactly \(2/\pi\).
MSE + QJL has slope 1.00 at every width, but its residual noise is roughly 1.5 to 2 times larger at the same total bits, because QJL gets one sign bit per coordinate while the MSE stage loses a bit of resolution.

Part 2 is what the model feels. The unbiased keys get the needle’s probability closer to the truth (0.509 against 0.534), but their noise lands on all 4095 other logits. The exponential in softmax turns zero-mean logit noise into a biased, heavier tail of spurious attention mass. Total-variation distance gets worse (0.118 against 0.081) and the output error is no better. A uniform shrinkage of every logit by the same factor is close to a temperature change, which softmax tolerates well. Independent noise per key is not.
This is not just a toy effect. vLLM’s TurboQuant integration omits QJL on purpose. Its documentation says the omission follows “community consensus (5+ independent groups)” that QJL “hurts attention quality by amplifying variance through softmax”. The RaBitQ authors’ comparison note (Section 10) cites the same observation. The paper’s own KV-cache experiments use the outlier-split bit allocation from Section 7. When you implement this for attention, start with the MSE variant plus norm correction.

title: TurboQuant: Rotate-then-Quantize KV Caches at 3 Bits
section: 7. Fractional bits and the outlier split
text:
7. Fractional bits and the outlier split
The paper’s “2.5-bit” and “3.5-bit” settings come from running two TurboQuant instances per head with different widths. For 2.5 bits, 32 outlier channels get 3 bits and the other 96 get 2: \((32 \cdot 3 + 96 \cdot 2)/128 = 2.5\). Rotation spreads outliers, but it does not make the extra bits worthless. Channels that are hot across the whole sequence are known ahead of time, and giving them more resolution is cheap. Each instance needs its own rotation over its own channel subset, and its own norm.
Values are a different problem. Keys meet a query in a dot product and then a softmax. Values are averaged with softmax weights, which already averages out independent errors. vLLM keeps keys on the rotate-and-Lloyd-Max path and stores values with plain uniform 3- or 4-bit quantization (scale and zero point per vector). Its turboquant_k8v4 preset goes further: FP8 keys with no rotation, and 4-bit values.

title: TurboQuant: Rotate-then-Quantize KV Caches at 3 Bits
section: 8. Kernel view: never un-rotate a key
text:
8. Kernel view: never un-rotate a key
A naive integration dequantizes the cache back to bf16 and calls the normal attention kernel. That spends HBM bandwidth on the decompressed copy, which defeats the point. The algebra allows something much better. With orthogonal \(\Pi\):
\[\langle q, \hat k\rangle = \lVert k\rVert\,\langle q, \Pi^\top c_{\text{idx}}\rangle = \lVert k\rVert\,\langle \Pi q, c_{\text{idx}}\rangle.\]
Rotate the query once per head. Then each key’s score is a table lookup (\(2^b\) centroids fit in registers) times the rotated query, times a norm. Values work the same way in reverse: accumulate \(\sum_i p_i \lVert v_i\rVert\, c_{\text{idx}_i}\) in the rotated basis and apply \(\Pi^\top\) once at the end.
# file: tq_rotated_domain.py
# Decode-time attention never has to un-rotate a key: rotate the query once instead.
# Values: accumulate the weighted codewords in the rotated domain, un-rotate once at the end.
import numpy as np

from tq_core import TurboQuantMSE

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n, d = 4096, 128
K, V, q = rng.standard_normal((n, d)), rng.standard_normal((n, d)), rng.standard_normal(d)
tqk, tqv = TurboQuantMSE(d, 3, rng), TurboQuantMSE(d, 3, rng)
k_idx, k_norm = tqk.quantize(K)
v_idx, v_norm = tqv.quantize(V)

# Reference: dequantize every key and value to full vectors (n inverse transforms each).
Kh, Vh = tqk.dequantize(k_idx, k_norm), tqv.dequantize(v_idx, v_norm)
s_ref = Kh @ q / np.sqrt(d)
p = np.exp(s_ref - s_ref.max())
p /= p.sum()
o_ref = p @ Vh

# Kernel form: one forward transform of q, table lookups per key, one inverse transform.
q_rot = tqk.rot.forward(q)                                   # once per (query, head)
s = k_norm[:, 0].astype(np.float64) * (tqk.centroids[k_idx] @ q_rot) / np.sqrt(d)
p2 = np.exp(s - s.max())
p2 /= p2.sum()
acc_rot = (p2 * v_norm[:, 0].astype(np.float64)) @ tqv.centroids[v_idx]   # stays rotated
o = tqv.rot.inverse(acc_rot)                                 # once per (query, head)

print(f"max |logit diff|  {np.abs(s - s_ref).max():.2e}")
print(f"max |output diff| {np.abs(o - o_ref).max():.2e}")
print(f"transforms per head: reference {2 * n}, rotated-domain 2")
python tq_rotated_domain.py
Output:
max |logit diff|  1.55e-15
max |output diff| 1.53e-16
transforms per head: reference 8192, rotated-domain 2
The two paths agree to machine precision. vLLM’s fused Triton decode kernel (triton_turboquant_decode.py) has this shape: it takes a precomputed Q_rot and scores packed 3- or 4-bit key indices against the centroid table inside the split-KV loop from the flash-decoding chapter. It does not rotate the value side, because its values are uniformly quantized.
The sign diagonal \(D\) is worth a look. vLLM’s current backend uses a plain Sylvester Hadamard, shared across layers. A code comment argues that random sign flips do not improve a symmetric Lloyd-Max quantizer. That is true for sign flips applied after the transform: a sign change mirrors a coordinate onto the mirror-image centroid. Signs applied before \(H\) are a different thing. They are what turns “works on typical inputs” into “works on every input”:
# file: tq_signs.py
# Plain Hadamard H x versus randomized Hadamard H D x in front of a 3-bit Lloyd-Max
# quantizer. On ordinary keys they tie. On inputs that line up with Walsh functions,
# the plain transform concentrates all the energy in one coordinate.
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import hadamard

from tq_core import fwht, lloyd_max_sphere

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
d, bits = 128, 3
c, edges, model = lloyd_max_sphere(d, bits)
signs = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=d)


def rel_err(x, randomize):
    u = x / np.linalg.norm(x, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    y = fwht(u * signs) if randomize else fwht(u)
    yh = c[np.searchsorted(edges, y)]
    uh = fwht(yh) * signs if randomize else fwht(yh)
    return np.mean(np.sum((u - uh) ** 2, 1))


scale = np.ones(d)
scale[[3, 17, 64, 101]] = [18.0, 12.0, 9.0, 15.0]
ordinary = rng.standard_normal((4096, d)) * scale
H = hadamard(d).astype(float)
walshy = H[rng.integers(0, d, 4096)] * 3.0 + 0.3 * rng.standard_normal((4096, d))

print(f"3-bit relative error (model {model:.4f})")
print(f"{'input':28} {'H x':>8} {'H D x':>8}")
for name, x in (("Gaussian + outlier channels", ordinary), ("near Walsh rows", walshy)):
    print(f"{name:28} {rel_err(x, False):8.4f} {rel_err(x, True):8.4f}")
python tq_signs.py
Output:
3-bit relative error (model 0.0340)
input                             H x    H D x
Gaussian + outlier channels    0.0300   0.0300
near Walsh rows                0.6813   0.0309
On ordinary keys the two transforms tie, which is why dropping \(D\) is a reasonable engineering choice. On inputs that correlate with Walsh functions, the plain transform maps nearly all the energy into one coordinate, and a codebook designed for \(\mathcal N(0, 1/d)\) clips it. A sign vector costs \(d\) bits per layer and one multiply per element. If you write your own kernel, keep it unless you have measured that your model’s keys never look like this.

It has Triton and (on ROCm) FlyDSL decode kernels, CI evaluation jobs per configuration, and boundary-layer protection (a configurable set of boundary layers skips compression). A follow-up PR for grouped 3/4-bit modes (#39890) was closed without merging. Note how fast the PPL cost grows below 4 bits on these presets. That is the honest version of “near-lossless at 3.5 bits”: it depends on outlier handling, the model, and the metric.
SGLang has had several TurboQuant PRs (#21419, #21617, #22048, #23135, and a ROCm variant #21628). All were closed without merging, so there is no upstream support in SGLang 0.5.21.
Speed claims. Google’s blog reports up to 8x faster attention-logit computation for 4-bit TurboQuant keys against 32-bit unquantized keys on H100. That is a kernel micro-benchmark against an fp32 baseline, not end-to-end decode against a bf16 or FP8 cache. Expect the end-to-end gain to come mostly from capacity (bigger batches, longer contexts) and from fewer HBM bytes in bandwidth-bound decode.

title: TurboQuant: Rotate-then-Quantize KV Caches at 3 Bits
section: 10. Credit where it is due: RaBitQ and the older rotation literature
text:
10. Credit where it is due: RaBitQ and the older rotation literature
Rotate-then-quantize is older than TurboQuant, and the paper’s treatment of prior work is disputed. State it plainly:

RaBitQ (Gao and Long, SIGMOD 2024, arXiv May 2024) and extended RaBitQ (arXiv September 2024, SIGMOD 2025) apply a random rotation and then quantize, with unbiased inner-product estimators and an error bound shown to be asymptotically optimal. On 27 March 2026, after Google’s blog post, RaBitQ’s first author said publicly that TurboQuant misdescribes RaBitQ’s method and guarantees, and that this had been raised with the authors before submission. He posted a public comment on the ICLR OpenReview page.
The RaBitQ authors’ technical note “Revisiting RaBitQ and TurboQuant” (arXiv:2604.19528) reruns both methods with their public code. On KV-cache tasks it reports clear RaBitQ gains at 2.5 bits and comparable results at 3.5 bits. For example, on needle-in-a-haystack with Llama-3.1-8B: full cache 0.987, RaBitQ 3.5-bit 0.977, TurboQuant-MSE 3.5-bit 0.962, RaBitQ 2.5-bit 0.951, TurboQuant-MSE 2.5-bit 0.709. It also reports that the paper’s runtime comparison ran the RaBitQ baseline single-threaded on a CPU, and that the speed claims did not reproduce. These are one party’s measurements. The code is public (VectorDB-NTU/rabitq-turboquant-comparison) so you can check them.
vLLM’s own module docstring credits DRIVE (NeurIPS 2021) and EDEN (ICML 2022) for the Hadamard-rotation-plus-scalar-quantization pattern. It notes the scheme is mathematically equivalent to the scalar case of HIGGS (NAACL 2025), and that “Cache Me If You Must” (ICML 2025) applied it to KV caches first. In weight and activation quantization, QuaRot, QuIP# and SpinQuant use the same rotation idea.

For a kernel engineer the practical takeaway is that the algorithm is a well-understood family, not one paper’s invention. Choose the variant by measured attention quality and kernel cost, and cite the lineage when you write it up.

Functional (CPU)

tq_codebook.py reproduces the distortion table. If 3-bit D is not about 0.034 at \(d=128\), the density or Lloyd iteration is wrong.

Attention-level diagnostics on real activations: logit RMSE, top-k overlap, and TV distance of attention distributions per layer. Layers that degrade most are candidates for boundary protection or more bits.

Decode throughput at fixed batch versus context length (where the cache dominates), and maximum batch at fixed memory.
Profile the store kernel separately. A slow quantize path shows up as prefill time, not decode time.

title: TurboQuant: Rotate-then-Quantize KV Caches at 3 Bits
text:
Summary
TurboQuant quantizes each KV vector by normalizing it, rotating it with a random orthogonal transform (a randomized Hadamard in practice), and rounding every coordinate with one Lloyd-Max codebook computed offline for the coordinate distribution of a random unit vector. The rotation removes outlier channels, and the fixed codebook removes per-block scales and calibration. The paper’s distortion numbers reproduce in a few lines of NumPy. The unbiased QJL variant is the wrong default inside softmax: shrinkage behaves like a temperature change, while per-key noise spreads attention mass, and production code (vLLM) omits QJL for that reason. A good decode kernel never decompresses the cache. It rotates the query and scores packed indices against a register-resident centroid table. vLLM ships 3- and 4-bit presets whose perplexity cost rises quickly below 4 bits, and SGLang has no merged implementation. The rotate-then-quantize idea comes from a lineage (DRIVE, EDEN, RaBitQ, HIGGS) whose credit is contested, so measure the variants yourself.

title: Mixture-of-Experts Kernels: Routing, Permutation, and Grouped GEMM
text:
Mixture-of-Experts Kernels: Routing, Permutation, and Grouped GEMM
Most frontier open-weight models are now Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi K2 have 256 and 384 routed experts per layer, Qwen3-235B-A22B and gpt-oss-120b have 128, and every token uses only 4 to 8 of them. The model holds hundreds of billions of parameters, but each token pays for only a few tens of billions. For a kernel engineer, that changes the central operation. Instead of one large GEMM per feed-forward layer, each layer runs dozens to hundreds of small GEMMs of different, data-dependent sizes, and the sizes are only known after the router has run on the GPU.
This chapter builds the MoE layer kernel by kernel. It writes a ground-truth reference, gets the routing semantics right (including the DeepSeek-style bias that is easy to misuse), builds the block-aligned indirection table that production kernels consume, writes a fused grouped GEMM in Triton that gathers and scatters rows itself, verifies it on a CPU with the Triton interpreter, compiles it for a Hopper GPU you do not own, and then uses shape arithmetic to explain why prefill and decode need different MoE kernels.

title: Mixture-of-Experts Kernels: Routing, Permutation, and Grouped GEMM
section: 1. Why MoE is a kernel problem
text:
1. Why MoE is a kernel problem
A dense SwiGLU feed-forward layer computes \(W_2\,(\mathrm{silu}(W_1x)\odot W_3x)\) with one weight set. An MoE layer has \(E\) such weight sets (the experts) plus a small router \(W_g\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times H}\). For each token, the router scores all experts, keeps the top \(k\), and the layer output is the weighted sum of those \(k\) experts’ outputs.

Three properties make this hard to run fast:

Ragged, data-dependent sizes. Expert \(e\) receives \(n_e\) token rows, with \(\sum_e n_e = T\cdot k\) for a batch of \(T\) tokens. The \(n_e\) change every step, live in GPU memory, and are often zero.
Weights dominate bytes. One DeepSeek-V3 expert is \(3HI\approx 44\) M parameters. Every active expert must stream its whole weight set from HBM, whether it serves one token or a thousand.
Imbalance. Routers are trained to balance load on average. Any given batch can still send most tokens to a few hot experts, and the slowest expert sets the latency of the layer.

The rest of the chapter is about turning “\(E\) ragged GEMMs” into one launch that keeps the tensor cores busy when there is enough work, and keeps HBM busy when there is not.
